papers.title: SwarmEvolve: Latent Agent Swarms for Evolutionary Discovery and Optimization
papers.abstract: LLM-guided evolutionary search uses AI agents to improve programs for mathematical and computational problems by iteratively refining solutions and combining high-scoring methods. However, the process is often slow because the LLM generates a long textual chain of thought for each round and must repeat this generation many times to maintain population diversity. We present SwarmEvolve, a framework in which hundreds of low-cost agents per round work in swarms, reason in latent space without decoding to text, and share information by passing KV caches. Each swarm studies the problem from a different angle. A novelty filter keeps the most distinct agent ideas by directly measuring the distances between the agents' hidden state vectors. Crossover of ideas happens naturally in latent space, as a summarizer agent receives the combined KV caches of all swarm members. On 21 problems in mathematical discovery and scientific computing, SwarmEvolve gets the highest average score and needs a median of only 3 to 8 minutes to reach the best scores that other state-of-the-art frameworks reach in 60 minutes. On several problems, SwarmEvolve with Qwen3 8B improves on the solutions that AlphaEvolve first found with frontier LLMs. Our work shows that agent swarms that communicate in latent space offer a fast, low-cost approach to program search for scientific problems.
papers.what_changed: The authors introduce SwarmEvolve, a framework where AI agents perform evolutionary search by reasoning directly in latent space and sharing KV caches rather than generating textual chains of thought. This approach achieves higher scores on 21 mathematical and scientific computing problems while reducing search time to 3 to 8 minutes compared to 60 minutes for existing state-of-the-art frameworks.
papers.why_it_matters: Researchers and practitioners looking to optimize scientific code can use this method to drastically reduce computational costs and latency in evolutionary searches without sacrificing solution quality.

explanations.plain: Imagine you have a team of researchers trying to solve a complex math problem. Usually, every researcher has to write a long, detailed report on their progress every time they want to share an idea. This takes a lot of time and slows everyone down. SwarmEvolve is like a team of researchers who have learned to communicate instantly using their raw thoughts instead of writing formal reports. By skipping the step of turning their ideas into written words, they can brainstorm, combine their strategies, and solve problems much faster. The system even uses a special filter to make sure the researchers are sharing unique ideas rather than just repeating the same thoughts, which helps them find the best solution much more quickly than standard methods.
explanations.student: SwarmEvolve shifts LLM-guided evolutionary search from token-level generation to latent space manipulation. In standard evolutionary search, models generate textual chains of thought (CoT) to evolve programs, which incurs high inference latency and high token consumption. This paper proposes a swarm-based architecture where agents process problems in latent space. Instead of decoding text, agents share information by passing Key-Value (KV) caches, the internal memory states of the transformer, between nodes. This allows for massive parallelism across hundreds of low-cost agents per generation. The framework utilizes a novelty filter that operates directly on the agents' hidden state vectors, effectively calculating distances in latent space to maintain population diversity. Crossover is achieved by a summarizer agent that aggregates the pooled KV caches. By bypassing the auto-regressive decoding step, the method achieves significant speedups, reaching optimal solutions in 3 to 8 minutes versus the hour-long runtime typically required by conventional frameworks. The results demonstrate that smaller models (Qwen3 8B) using this latent swarm strategy can outperform larger frontier models on scientific and mathematical benchmarks.
explanations.expert: SwarmEvolve addresses the latency bottlenecks in LLM-driven evolutionary search by replacing textual CoT with latent space reasoning. The framework operates via multi-agent swarms that utilize KV cache passing to communicate without autoregressive decoding. Diversity is managed via a latent novelty filter, which computes Euclidean distances between hidden state representations to prune redundant agents. The crossover operation is formalized through a summarizer agent that performs aggregation over the union of swarm KV caches. Benchmarked across 21 mathematical and scientific computing tasks, SwarmEvolve exhibits a superior Pareto frontier compared to state-of-the-art baselines. Specifically, it achieves a median runtime of 3 to 8 minutes, representing an order-of-magnitude reduction from the 60-minute duration characteristic of standard frameworks. Notably, the framework enables a Qwen3 8B model to surpass solutions previously established by AlphaEvolve using frontier-class models. The approach demonstrates that latent-level interactions effectively circumvent the O(n) decoding overhead, providing an efficient alternative for large-scale program search. Limitations include dependence on the capacity of the latent space to represent complex program modifications and the sensitivity of the summarizer agent to incoming cache noise.

papers.title: Scientist World: Grow a Research World for AI-Scientists
papers.abstract: AI-Scientists arrived, but a world for them to grow in did not. Human scientists take theirs for granted $-$ centuries of open problems and shared ideas, waiting in the scientific literature. To AI-Scientists, that world is readable but not runnable, so we build Scientist World for them: every research paper becomes an executable environment. Our autonomous pipeline extracts each paper's open-ended research question and reproduces its proposed method as the baseline; an AI-Scientist entering the environment is evaluated against what the human authors achieved. We release the first 1,000 verified environments. With the world as an evaluation, we found that frontier AI-Scientists can already surpass the human researchers 74% of the time. As a record of how AI does science, it contains 6,400 hours of research traces, with every idea, experiment, failure, and success. As a training ground, we are able to raise (+158%) a small model to match frontier models in research ideation. At last, AI-Scientists' own world has arrived, grown from and growing with science itself.
papers.what_changed: The authors introduce Scientist World, a framework that converts research papers into executable environments where AI-Scientists can perform research, alongside a dataset of 1,000 verified environments and 6,400 hours of research traces.
papers.why_it_matters: It provides a standardized, runnable playground to evaluate and train autonomous AI agents in scientific research tasks, moving beyond static literature to active experimentation.

explanations.plain: AI researchers currently read papers, but they cannot easily test their ideas in the same environments used by the original authors. Think of Scientist World like a digital science fair that turns every academic paper into a playable game level. Instead of just reading about a discovery, an AI agent can step into the paper's specific challenge and try to solve it itself. The researchers built 1,000 of these interactive 'levels' where AI agents can experiment, fail, and succeed just like human scientists. By tracking these attempts, the team created a massive record of how AI thinks through problems. This allows AI to practice doing science in a safe space, helping machines improve their own ability to come up with new ideas and solve complex research puzzles.
explanations.student: Scientist World is an environment framework designed to bridge the gap between static research literature and executable code for autonomous AI agents. The core challenge is that while AI-Scientists can parse text, they lack a standardized sandbox to validate hypotheses against existing benchmarks. This system automates a pipeline that extracts research questions from papers and sets up the corresponding method as a baseline environment for evaluation. The authors provide 1,000 such environments and a dataset of 6,400 hours of research traces, essentially logs of AI-driven exploration, including failed experiments and successful iterations. This acts as both a rigorous benchmark, where AI performance is measured against human-reported results, and a training ground for imitation learning. The study reports that frontier AI models outperform humans in these environments 74% of the time. Furthermore, the dataset enables the fine-tuning of smaller models, yielding a 158% improvement in research ideation performance, allowing smaller, more efficient models to compete with frontier-class systems in generating scientific concepts.
explanations.expert: Scientist World provides a standardized evaluation infrastructure for autonomous research agents by converting academic papers into executable research environments. The framework features an autonomous pipeline that parses papers to extract research questions and formalize proposed methods into baselines, enabling quantitative evaluation against human-reported benchmarks. The release includes 1,000 verified environments and 6,400 hours of research trajectories, which capture the latent search space and decision-making processes of agents. Empirical evaluation demonstrates that frontier AI-Scientists outperform human researchers in 74% of the curated tasks. Additionally, the authors utilize these traces to improve research ideation, showing a 158% performance gain in smaller models when fine-tuned on the provided logs, effectively closing the gap with larger frontier models in scientific reasoning tasks. The primary technical contribution is the systemic transformation of unstructured text into a structured, executable, and reproducible environment for agentic evaluation, addressing the long-standing reproducibility crisis in autonomous research agent development.

papers.title: Social Humanoid: Socially Responsive Human-Humanoid Interaction
papers.abstract: Humanoid robots are typically trained as solitary agents, leaving them unable to coordinate physically with human partners who naturally anticipate and adjust to one another. To bridge this gap, we present Social Humanoid, a hierarchical system that generates and executes socially responsive whole-body motion on a 29-DoF Unitree G1 conditioned on a human partner's motion. Its high-level policy performs flexible sequence modeling of human and humanoid motion through a shared tokenized representation, generating reactive humanoid motion and anticipating the partner's motion when they are occluded, while a low-level whole-body tracking controller executes the generated motion on the robot. To train the system, we introduce a two-phase adaptive retargeting procedure that retargets one interaction partner to the robot while morphing the other partner to preserve contact dynamics, reachability, and relative body scale. We apply this procedure across five motion-capture datasets to produce a new Human-Humanoid Interaction (HHI) benchmark of 260 hours of human-humanoid interactions. Our results demonstrate that Social Humanoid produces coordinated, human-aligned behavior across diverse interaction types in simulation and the real world. Project page: https://von31.github.io/social-humanoid/
papers.what_changed: The authors introduce Social Humanoid, a hierarchical framework for socially responsive whole-body motion on a 29-DoF Unitree G1 robot, trained using a novel two-phase adaptive retargeting procedure that converts human-human interaction data into 260 hours of human-humanoid interaction sequences.
papers.why_it_matters: Researchers and robotics engineers should care because this work enables humanoid robots to move in sync with humans, moving beyond solitary navigation toward fluid physical collaboration.

explanations.plain: Most robots today act like strangers in a crowd. They might move around people, but they do not really interact or dance with them. Imagine trying to waltz with someone who is always looking at their phone and ignoring your lead. It would be clumsy and frustrating. The researchers built a new system called Social Humanoid that helps robots act more like a natural dance partner. By watching thousands of hours of humans interacting, the robot learned to predict what a person will do next, even if they step behind an obstacle, and adjust its own body movements to stay in sync. This means in the future, your robot assistant could high-five you, hand you a tool, or walk beside you with human-like grace.
explanations.student: Social Humanoid is a hierarchical control framework designed to enable socially reactive motion in a 29-degree-of-freedom humanoid (Unitree G1). The system separates the task into two layers: a high-level policy and a low-level whole-body controller. The high-level policy utilizes a shared tokenized representation to model sequences of both human and humanoid motion, allowing for anticipatory action even when the human partner is occluded. The low-level controller translates these generated motions into precise motor commands. A primary innovation is the two-phase adaptive retargeting procedure, which transforms existing human-human motion capture data into humanoid-compatible training data. This process carefully morphs the secondary partner to maintain physical constraints like contact dynamics, relative body scale, and reachability. By applying this to five motion-capture datasets, the authors created a 260-hour benchmark of Human-Humanoid Interaction (HHI). This approach overcomes the limitations of solitary agent training by explicitly conditioning the humanoid's policy on human motion trajectories, facilitating smoother, more responsive collaboration.
explanations.expert: The Social Humanoid framework addresses the challenge of collaborative humanoid locomotion and interaction. The system architecture is hierarchical: a Transformer-based high-level policy performs sequence modeling in a shared tokenized space, enabling reactive and predictive motion generation. This policy is conditioned on human pose sequences. The low-level controller employs whole-body tracking to ensure the robot adheres to the high-level trajectory while respecting kinematics. The core methodological contribution is a two-phase adaptive retargeting algorithm, which adapts human-human interaction data to the Unitree G1 morphology. Phase one maps one agent's kinematics to the robot; phase two utilizes a morphing technique to preserve spatial relationships, reachability, and contact manifolds between the humanoid and the remaining human agent. This yielded a 260-hour HHI dataset across five motion-capture sources. Empirical evaluation demonstrates effective cross-domain transfer from simulation to the real-world Unitree G1, characterized by high-fidelity tracking and temporal coordination. The primary limitation is the inherent complexity of high-degree-of-freedom whole-body control and the dependence on the quality of the motion-capture source distribution for handling diverse interaction types.

papers.title: BabyTheorist: A Benchmark for Learning to Theorize the World from Observation Alone
papers.abstract: How would we know whether a machine truly understands the world? We argue that one key capability is \textit{observational theory learning}: acquiring reusable theories from pure observations and applying them to new situations. Current visual reasoning benchmarks focus primarily on the latter, presenting each task as a few-shot puzzle grouped by a common rule. We introduce BabyTheorist, a benchmark for controlled training and evaluation of observational theory learning. BabyTheorist generates continual streams of before-after visual observations from hidden compositional programs; during training, learners see only the resulting transitions, with no program labels, task identities, or support sets. To support theory learning and evaluation, BabyTheorist controls the program language, a curriculum over program complexity, recurring frequent subprograms, and a continual train-test protocol with level skipping. Seven representative baselines plateau well below ceiling, with the gap widening as the curriculum advances---evidence that BabyTheorist isolates a capability current program-learning approaches do not yet address.
papers.what_changed: The authors introduce BabyTheorist, a benchmark that requires models to learn reusable theories from continuous visual observations without explicit program labels or task identity, testing the ability to infer hidden compositional programs from transitions alone.
papers.why_it_matters: It targets a gap in current AI research, specifically moving beyond static few-shot puzzles to test if machines can genuinely understand the underlying rules of a world through observation alone, a prerequisite for human-like reasoning.

explanations.plain: Imagine you are watching a game for the first time without anyone explaining the rules. Over time, you notice patterns, like why a player moves a certain way or when a point is scored, and you eventually form your own theory about how the game works. This is exactly what the BabyTheorist benchmark tests in computers. Most current AI programs are given puzzles with clear instructions or labels, which is like solving a math problem with the answer key provided. BabyTheorist removes those hints. It shows the computer a continuous stream of events and sees if the machine can figure out the hidden 'laws' governing those events on its own. It is a new way to measure if a computer is actually learning how the world functions.
explanations.student: BabyTheorist is a novel benchmark designed to evaluate 'observational theory learning,' which the authors define as the ability to induce reusable, compositional rules from raw, unlabeled state transitions. Unlike standard visual reasoning tasks that rely on few-shot paradigms or explicit rule-based puzzles (like Raven's Progressive Matrices or CLEVR), this benchmark provides a continuous stream of before-after visual observations. The learner must infer the underlying 'hidden programs' responsible for these transitions without access to task IDs or support sets. The framework systematically controls the program language, introduces a curriculum for increasing complexity, and incorporates recurring subprograms to facilitate generalization. By using a continual train-test protocol with 'level skipping,' it forces models to demonstrate that they have internalized the theory rather than just memorizing specific task instances. The current state-of-the-art results show that seven representative baselines fail to achieve ceiling performance, with the gap between model performance and the optimal solution increasing as the complexity of the program curriculum advances. This suggests that existing program-learning architectures lack the necessary inductive biases to extract abstract, compositional rules from observational data.
explanations.expert: BabyTheorist introduces a benchmark to measure observational theory learning, shifting from static few-shot reasoning to a continuous, unlabeled observation protocol. The setup generates visual transitions based on hidden compositional programs. Crucially, the system prohibits access to task identities, labels, or support sets, forcing the learner to perform latent structure discovery and rule induction. The benchmark implements a rigorous curriculum over program complexity and employs frequent subprogram injection to test compositional reuse. The methodology includes a continual evaluation protocol with level skipping to prevent overfitting to specific curriculum stages. Experimental results evaluated across seven baselines indicate significant performance degradation as the program complexity increases, with all models plateauing well below the theoretical ceiling. This performance gap underscores a limitation in contemporary program induction and visual representation learning approaches, which often rely on structural guidance that is absent in this environment. The benchmark highlights that current systems struggle to map raw observational streams into robust, transferable symbolic or latent theories, providing a quantitative metric for assessing the maturity of world-model acquisition in autonomous agents.

papers.title: Failure Prediction and Classification in Vision-Language-Action Models Via Calibrated Latent Probing
papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) enable general-purpose embodied intelligence, but their performance is brittle under distribution shift, where unanticipated failures can damage equipment or endanger people. Deploying VLAs in real-world systems therefore requires a runtime monitor that is timely, calibrated, and informative while being efficient enough to run on the edge. Existing methods fail to fulfill these requirements. We present VLA-Tug, a lightweight probe over the latent layers of a VLA backbone that improves early failure detection and bounds the missed-detection and false-alarm rates, with minimal inference overhead. We show that supervising on the pre-failure segment of a trajectory increases early failure detection at matched false-positive rates by up to 30% over the strongest learned baseline. Under shift to unseen tasks, the bounds on missed-detection and false-alarm rates remain valid in up to 86% of runs, versus at most 21% for baselines. Unlike existing methods, VLA-Tug predicts the failure mode to enable corrective actions, raising top-3 accuracy on unseen tasks by up to 44% over a majority baseline. VLA-Tug enables real-time monitoring where the well-timed and informative probe supports lightweight steering that improves task success. We release a dataset of 3,180 annotated manipulation episodes to support future work on latent failure detection in VLAs at https://vla-tug.github.io.
papers.what_changed: The authors introduce VLA-Tug, a lightweight latent probe designed for real-time failure prediction and classification in Vision-Language-Action models, achieving up to 30% higher early detection and 44% higher top-3 failure classification accuracy on unseen tasks compared to baselines.
papers.why_it_matters: Engineers and researchers deploying embodied AI in real-world environments need reliable, efficient safety monitors to prevent damage and enable corrective actions when models encounter unexpected situations.

explanations.plain: Vision-Language-Action models help robots perform tasks by understanding visual data and natural language instructions. However, these models can sometimes get confused when they face new environments, leading to mistakes that might cause damage. To fix this, researchers developed VLA-Tug, a safety tool that acts like a backseat driver. It constantly checks the robot's internal 'thought process', represented as latent layers, to predict if the robot is about to make a mistake before it happens. Think of it like a smart sensor in a car that detects if a driver is getting sleepy and warns them before an accident occurs. Because it is lightweight, this tool can run directly on the robot's computer, helping it avoid errors and stay on track in new, unfamiliar tasks.
explanations.student: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models combine visual processing with language instruction to drive embodied agents. A major challenge is 'distribution shift,' where the model encounters scenarios outside its training data, leading to brittle performance. VLA-Tug addresses this by implementing a lightweight probing mechanism on the model's internal latent representations. By supervising the probe on pre-failure trajectory segments, the system learns to predict failure modes before they manifest. This is significant because it provides early detection and, crucially, failure classification, identifying *why* a failure might happen. The system maintains formal bounds on missed-detection and false-alarm rates, which is a common challenge in safety-critical robotics. Evaluation on 3,180 annotated manipulation episodes shows that VLA-Tug significantly outperforms learned baselines, improving early detection by 30% and failure mode classification accuracy by 44% on unseen tasks. By keeping the probe computationally efficient, the authors enable real-time steering and intervention, making it practical for edge deployment in robotic systems where latency and resource constraints are primary concerns.
explanations.expert: VLA-Tug addresses the challenge of runtime failure monitoring in Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models. The method utilizes a lightweight latent probe trained on pre-failure trajectories to provide predictive insights into model reliability. In empirical evaluation, VLA-Tug achieved a 30% increase in early failure detection over learned baselines at matched false-positive rates. A key differentiator is the method's ability to classify failure modes, resulting in a 44% improvement in top-3 classification accuracy for unseen tasks. The approach demonstrates superior robustness under distribution shift; the predicted bounds on missed-detection and false-alarm rates hold in up to 86% of runs, compared to a maximum of 21% for baselines. The architecture is optimized for edge deployment, ensuring the inference overhead remains minimal to support real-time steering. The study introduces a dataset of 3,180 manipulation episodes, providing a benchmark for latent failure detection. Limitations include dependency on the quality of latent representations for failure state discernment and potential performance variance based on the underlying VLA backbone capacity.

papers.title: Data-driven discovery of intrinsic Lie point symmetries of differential equation systems
papers.abstract: Discovering continuous symmetries directly from differential-equation data can reveal geometric structure for model reduction and scientific machine learning without symbolic determining equations or a closed-form representation of the governing system. We formulate intrinsic Lie point-symmetry discovery as an operator-theoretic problem on sampled jet-space data. Admissible generators are identified from a sampled determining operator and separated from redundant, solution-dependent, and geometrically trivial directions. The framework combines prolongation, sequential subspace restrictions, and a fixed nonlinear dictionary linear in trainable coefficients. A rank-stabilization preflight test diagnoses systems whose represented intrinsic symmetry algebra does not stabilize under dictionary refinement. On a controlled differential-equation benchmark with an analytically known 11-dimensional represented intrinsic symmetry algebra, the method recovers the complete represented generator set, reproduces its Lie-bracket structure to numerical precision, and approximates a known generator beyond the training domain. Here we show that explicit intrinsic continuous-symmetry generators can be recovered from data obtained from exact or approximate differential systems.
papers.what_changed: The authors introduce a data-driven framework for discovering intrinsic Lie point symmetries directly from differential equation data, avoiding the need for symbolic equations. The method uses an operator-theoretic approach on jet-space data, employing prolongation and sequential subspace restrictions to identify generators.
papers.why_it_matters: This approach enables scientists to uncover hidden geometric structures in physical systems even when the underlying symbolic equations are unknown, facilitating better model reduction and scientific machine learning.

explanations.plain: Imagine you are trying to understand the rules of a game just by watching players move pieces on a board. Sometimes, the game has hidden patterns, like a rule that says if you move a piece one way, the whole board rotates but the game stays the same. In mathematics, these are called symmetries. Scientists usually find these by solving complex equations, which is hard. This paper introduces a way to find these hidden patterns just by looking at the data from a system. It works like a digital detective that scans the data to see how it moves and shifts, then identifies the rules governing those movements. This helps researchers simplify complex problems without needing to know the exact mathematical formulas beforehand.
explanations.student: In differential equations, Lie point symmetries are continuous transformations that map solutions to solutions, preserving the structure of the system. Traditionally, finding these requires solving symbolic 'determining equations,' which is computationally expensive or impossible for complex systems. This paper reframes symmetry discovery as an operator-theoretic problem. By working in 'jet-space', a mathematical space that captures both the coordinates and their derivatives, the authors represent symmetry generators as operators. The method utilizes a fixed nonlinear dictionary to parameterize these operators. To ensure the discovered generators are meaningful, the authors apply a rank-stabilization test, which filters out redundant or trivial components. The framework uses prolongation (extending transformations to derivatives) and sequential subspace restrictions to isolate valid generators. In experiments using a benchmark system with an 11-dimensional symmetry algebra, the model successfully recovered the full set of generators and maintained the correct Lie-bracket structure, which defines the algebra's closure properties. This is a significant advancement in scientific machine learning (SciML), moving toward model-free discovery of geometric invariants.
explanations.expert: The authors propose an operator-theoretic formulation for discovering intrinsic Lie point symmetries from sampled jet-space data, bypassing symbolic determining equations. The framework identifies admissible symmetry generators by analyzing a sampled determining operator constructed from a nonlinear dictionary of functions. The optimization objective is linear in trainable coefficients, allowing for the isolation of true symmetry generators from trivial or solution-dependent artifacts. Key to the architecture is a rank-stabilization preflight test that evaluates the convergence of the represented symmetry algebra under dictionary refinement. Experimental validation on a benchmark differential system with an 11-dimensional intrinsic Lie algebra shows the method recovers the complete generator set, reconstructs the Lie-bracket structure to high numerical precision, and demonstrates generalization by approximating a generator beyond the training distribution. The primary limitation is the reliance on the quality of sampled jet-space data and the completeness of the nonlinear dictionary. By operating directly on observational data, the framework provides a robust path for identifying geometric structures in systems where symbolic representations are unavailable or analytically intractable.

papers.title: Identifying Neural Dynamics Using Nonlinear Interventional State Space Models
papers.abstract: State-space models (SSMs) recover low-dimensional latent dynamics from high-dimensional observations, but latents are generally not identifiable from observational data alone. Interventional state-space models (iSSMs) use perturbations to break observational symmetries and identify parameters up to permutation, scaling, and shift. However, prior work restricts identifiability to linear latent dynamics and piecewise-linear emissions, excluding many behaviors characteristic of neural circuits. We extend iSSMs to a substantially broader model class: we prove that (i) affine identifiability holds under general injective emission functions and Gaussian latent transitions, and (ii) with interventions, identifiability up to permutation, scaling, and shift is preserved under general nonlinear latent dynamics. We validate our theory on simulated FitzHugh-Nagumo dynamics, and then demonstrate two applications: adjudicating between competing models of decision-making; and predicting responses to unseen micro-stimulation in macaque and human neural recordings, with proof-of-concept generalization to a held-out stimulation site in the latter. Finally, simulations yield practical guidance for designing stimulation protocols that improve identifiability.
papers.what_changed: The authors extend interventional state-space models (iSSMs) to support nonlinear latent dynamics and general injective emission functions, proving that these models remain identifiable up to permutation, scaling, and shift.
papers.why_it_matters: Researchers studying neural circuits can now reliably uncover hidden brain states and dynamics using nonlinear models, which previously were often unidentifiable without specific linear constraints.

explanations.plain: Imagine you are trying to understand how a complex machine works by watching it run from the outside. If you only watch it, many different internal settings could explain the same outward behavior, making it impossible to know the truth. This is a common problem in neuroscience when looking at brain recordings. Scientists often use 'interventions', like nudging the machine to see how it reacts, to narrow down the possibilities. This paper introduces a new way to mathematically decode these hidden inner workings even when the machine's internal parts move in complex, curvy, non-straight ways. Think of it like finally having the right map to interpret how a person’s thoughts translate into actions by specifically testing which 'levers' in the brain cause which reactions.
explanations.student: In neuroscience and time-series analysis, state-space models (SSMs) aim to recover latent variables from high-dimensional observations. A major theoretical hurdle is 'identifiability': determining if the recovered latent states uniquely correspond to the true underlying system or are just an arbitrary transformation. While linear iSSMs solve this by using interventional data, systematic perturbations, to break observational symmetries, they fail to capture the complex, nonlinear dynamics inherent in biological neural circuits. This paper expands the scope of identifiable iSSMs by providing proofs for affine identifiability under general injective emission functions and nonlinear latent transitions. The authors confirm these theoretical findings by validating them on FitzHugh-Nagumo dynamics, a common model for neural spiking. Practically, this means that given enough interventional data, we can recover the true latent structure of a system even when both the emission model and the transition dynamics are nonlinear. This work offers a rigorous framework for applying state-space modeling to neural data, moving beyond the restrictive linear assumptions that have historically limited latent variable discovery in complex dynamical systems.
explanations.expert: The authors address the identifiability of latent variables in state-space models (SSMs) by generalizing the interventional framework (iSSMs). Prior work on iSSMs was largely restricted to linear latent transitions and piecewise-linear emissions. The authors prove two main results: first, that affine identifiability is maintained under general injective emission functions with Gaussian latent transitions; and second, that identifiability up to permutation, scaling, and shift is preserved under general nonlinear latent dynamics when interventional data is available. The paper validates these proofs using simulated FitzHugh-Nagumo dynamics. Application experiments include adjudicating between competing models of decision-making and predicting micro-stimulation responses in macaque and human neural data. Notably, the authors achieve proof-of-concept generalization to a held-out stimulation site in human recordings, demonstrating the practical utility of their framework. The paper concludes by providing heuristic guidance for experimental design, specifically how to structure stimulation protocols to maximize parameter identifiability. Limitations are inherent to the necessity of interventional data, as the system relies on the assumption of injecting known perturbations into the latent space to break the symmetries that otherwise render nonlinear latent dynamics unidentifiable from observational data alone.

papers.title: Muir: Linear Attention with Sensitivity-Allocated Gating and Matched-Filter Readout
papers.abstract: Linear attention compresses context into a fixed-size key-value state for linear-time training and constant-memory inference. Gated delta-rule models decay this state and erase its prediction for an incoming key before writing a new value; Gated DeltaNet-2 (GDN-2) generalizes this with channel-wise decay and decoupled, full-rank erase and write gates. However, we show that state updates are far less sensitive to erasure than to writes: key activation and unit normalization concentrate key energy onto a sparse subset of channels, whereas value writes scale all channels, so the erase gate can be parameterized at lower rank. Furthermore, slow-decaying state rows accumulate much larger norms than fast rows, dominating unweighted readout and forcing stronger write-time erasure to suppress interference. Guided by this analysis, we introduce Muir, which fuses all gates into a sensitivity-allocated low-rank projection, re-weights state rows with a matched-filter readout gate, and reinvests the saved parameters in a wider feed-forward network. Because standard chunkwise algorithms become numerically unstable at the large chunk sizes needed to saturate wide matrix units, we design a parallel update for stable, efficient training. Across 166M-1.34B parameters, Muir lowers perplexity by 1.8-2.0% over GDN-2 and 2.5-3.6% over Transformer, raises commonsense accuracy by up to 1.9 points, and improves extractive recall over GDN-2. At 1.34B, Muir outperforms both baselines on multi-hop and multi-needle recall, extrapolates 2,560x from its 4K training length to 10M-token streams without perplexity drift, and maintains near-100% passkey retrieval to 1M tokens with static readout. Muir achieves these gains while matching GDN-2 throughput, reaching its 100B-token validation loss 1.2x faster, and training 2.7x faster than Transformer at 32K.
papers.what_changed: Muir introduces a linear attention mechanism that uses sensitivity-allocated low-rank gate projections and matched-filter readouts to improve state updates. It replaces standard gate parameterization with a method that accounts for the imbalance between write sensitivity and erasure sensitivity in the model state.
papers.why_it_matters: Researchers and engineers building large language models will find Muir valuable because it achieves better perplexity and recall than Transformer and Gated DeltaNet models while enabling massive sequence length extrapolation without performance drift.

explanations.plain: Modern AI models often struggle to remember long sequences of information without using massive amounts of computer memory. Linear attention is a technique that acts like a compact notebook, summarizing past information into a fixed-size state. However, previous versions of this notebook were inefficient because they treated all information as equally important, leading to messy, inaccurate notes. Muir is an improvement that acts like a smarter editor. It realizes that some parts of the notebook are more sensitive to new data than others. By organizing how information is added, removed, and read, Muir makes the notebook much more precise. Think of it like a library index card system where you only update the most relevant categories instead of rewriting every card every time a new book arrives.
explanations.student: Muir addresses the limitations of linear attention mechanisms like Gated DeltaNet-2 (GDN-2), which map context into a fixed-size hidden state for linear-time training. The authors perform an empirical sensitivity analysis revealing that state updates are more sensitive to writes than erasures. Specifically, activation concentration limits key energy to sparse channels, while slow-decaying state rows tend to dominate the unweighted readout, causing interference. To mitigate this, Muir implements sensitivity-allocated low-rank projections for gating and a matched-filter readout that re-weights state rows. The model also includes a numerically stable parallel update algorithm designed to handle large chunk sizes, allowing for efficient training on wide matrix units. By optimizing the gate parameterization, the authors reinvest saved parameters into wider feed-forward networks. The results are significant: Muir demonstrates superior performance across parameters ranging from 166M to 1.34B, achieving a 1.8-2.0% perplexity reduction over GDN-2 and up to 3.6% over standard Transformers. Crucially, it demonstrates robust extrapolation, scaling from 4K training tokens to 10M-token streams without perplexity drift and maintaining high passkey retrieval accuracy at 1M tokens, all while providing faster training throughput compared to traditional Transformer architectures.
explanations.expert: Muir advances state-space-like linear attention by optimizing the gating dynamics of the GDN-2 framework. The authors observe that in existing gated delta-rule models, state sensitivity is non-uniform; write operations require higher rank parameterization than erasure due to the concentration of key energy. Furthermore, the accumulation of larger norms in slow-decaying state rows leads to interference during unweighted readout. Muir resolves this by fusing gating operations into a sensitivity-allocated low-rank projection and introducing a matched-filter readout gate to re-balance state row contributions. To facilitate the use of wide matrix units, the paper introduces a numerically stable parallel update algorithm that avoids the instabilities of traditional chunkwise approaches. Evaluated on 166M to 1.34B parameter models, Muir consistently outperforms GDN-2 and Transformers, showing a 1.8-3.6% perplexity improvement and gains in extractive recall and multi-hop reasoning. The model exhibits extreme context extrapolation, maintaining near 100% passkey retrieval up to 1M tokens with static readouts and scaling to 10M tokens without drift. While maintaining GDN-2 throughput, Muir achieves 100B-token validation loss 1.2x faster than GDN-2 and trains 2.7x faster than Transformers at 32K context lengths, providing a highly scalable alternative for long-sequence modeling.

papers.title: SpecCTMC: Exact Speculative Simulation of Diffusion Language Model Continuous-Time Markov Chains
papers.abstract: Masked diffusion language models offer parallel text generation, but independently sampling multiple tokens can disrupt their dependencies and change the output distribution. Exact continuous-time sampling avoids this approximation, yet typically requires one sequential model evaluation per token. We introduce SpecCTMC, a training-free speculative sampler that reduces this sequential bottleneck without a separate draft model. SpecCTMC proposes successive token updates using previously computed model predictions, evaluates their intermediate states in parallel, and applies an exact acceptance-and-correction procedure. We prove that SpecCTMC preserves the joint distribution of event times, generation order, and token values of the underlying continuous-time Markov chain. It therefore introduces neither time-discretization error nor additional factorization error from parallel decoding. Experiments on LLaDA-8B-Instruct and Dream-v0-Instruct-7B across five benchmarks demonstrate 1.73-4.38x fewer sequential model evaluations than direct continuous-time sampling, while preserving the reference sampling distribution. Our code is available at: https://github.com/kasakh/specctmc
papers.what_changed: SpecCTMC is a new training-free speculative sampler that reduces sequential model evaluations for diffusion language models by using previous model predictions for parallel token updates, while using an acceptance-and-correction mechanism to remain mathematically exact.
papers.why_it_matters: It allows for faster text generation in diffusion-based language models without sacrificing the quality or the exactness of the output distribution, which is a major bottleneck for these models.

explanations.plain: Modern AI language models that use a method called 'diffusion' are excellent at creating text, but they have a speed problem. To keep the text coherent, they often have to work one step at a time, which is slow. Think of this like a group of people trying to write a story together. If they wait for each other to finish every single word before writing the next, it takes a long time. SpecCTMC is a new technique that lets the AI 'guess' several words in advance based on what it already knows, check those guesses simultaneously, and then correct any mistakes. This allows the AI to write much faster while ensuring the story remains perfectly logical, just as if it had written it one word at a time.
explanations.student: Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) generate text by modeling the transition of data through a continuous-time process, typically structured as a Continuous-Time Markov Chain (CTMC). Traditionally, exact sampling from these chains is computationally expensive because it requires sequential evaluation of the model for every single token update, creating a significant latency bottleneck. SpecCTMC addresses this by implementing a speculative sampling strategy. Instead of requiring a separate, smaller 'draft' model, which is common in speculative decoding for autoregressive transformers, SpecCTMC reuses previous model computations to propose multiple successive token updates. These proposals are evaluated in parallel. The core contribution is an acceptance-and-correction procedure that ensures the output precisely matches the joint distribution of the underlying CTMC. By avoiding time-discretization errors and factorization errors, the method preserves the statistical rigor of the original model. In experiments with models like LLaDA-8B and Dream-v0-7B, the authors report a speedup of 1.73x to 4.38x in terms of the number of required sequential model evaluations compared to standard direct sampling methods.
explanations.expert: SpecCTMC introduces an exact speculative sampling framework for Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) defined over Continuous-Time Markov Chains (CTMCs). The primary challenge in CTMC-based DLMs is the sequential nature of sampling, where each state transition requires a model forward pass. SpecCTMC circumvents this without the need for an external draft model or auxiliary training. It operates by generating multiple token update proposals based on cached model predictions, parallelizing the state evaluation, and applying a formal acceptance-and-correction mechanism to maintain the exactness of the target distribution. The authors provide proofs that the method preserves the joint distribution of event times, generation order, and token states, effectively eliminating time-discretization and parallel decoding factorization errors. Empirical validation on LLaDA-8B-Instruct and Dream-v0-Instruct-7B across five standard benchmarks demonstrates a reduction in sequential model evaluations by a factor of 1.73x to 4.38x. This approach is strictly training-free, making it highly portable to existing pre-trained diffusion architectures that rely on CTMC-based inference. Limitations are inherent to the speculative overhead, which requires sufficient GPU memory to handle parallel intermediate state evaluations, though this is offset by the reduction in the total number of sequential passes required.

papers.title: Non-Parametric Mutual Information Estimation with Vine Copulas
papers.abstract: We introduce VINE: a non-parametric mutual information (MI) estimator based on simplified D-vine copulas. Approximating the joint density with a simplified D-vine allows the density ratio to simplify to a product of pair copulas, which we can estimate non-parametrically. This structural simplification yields VINE, a flexible and computationally efficient MI estimator. We compare VINE against SotA neural MI estimators on a range of datasets, both under settings where the simplified D-vine assumption holds and where it is violated, demonstrating competitive accuracy at a lower computational cost for low- to medium-dimensional datasets.
papers.what_changed: The authors introduce VINE, a non-parametric mutual information estimator that uses simplified D-vine copulas to decompose the joint density into a product of pair copulas.
papers.why_it_matters: Researchers and practitioners dealing with low- to medium-dimensional data can achieve competitive mutual information estimation accuracy with significantly lower computational costs compared to current neural network-based approaches.

explanations.plain: Mutual information is a way to measure how much information two variables share. If you know the weather, how much does that tell you about the likelihood of rain? Usually, calculating this is difficult because complex data has many intertwined relationships. This paper introduces a tool called VINE that breaks these complex relationships down into smaller, simpler parts using a structure called a Vine Copula. Think of it like trying to solve a complicated jigsaw puzzle by grouping pieces into smaller, manageable patterns rather than looking at all of them at once. By simplifying the math, VINE provides accurate results faster than traditional computer-based estimation methods that rely on heavy neural networks, especially when the data has a moderate number of variables.
explanations.student: Mutual information (MI) measures the statistical dependence between two random variables, often serving as a foundational metric in information theory and machine learning. Calculating MI requires estimating the joint probability density, which is notoriously difficult in high dimensions. This paper introduces VINE, a non-parametric estimator that leverages simplified D-vine copulas. A vine copula is a flexible graphical model that decomposes a multivariate distribution into a product of bivariate copulas, which describe the dependency structure between pairs of variables. By applying the 'simplifying assumption', a common approximation in copula modeling, the authors represent the density ratio required for MI as a product of pair-copula densities. This approach avoids the high computational overhead of training deep neural networks for density estimation. Students should note that while this method provides an efficient alternative, its performance relies on the validity of the D-vine structure. It performs competitively against state-of-the-art neural MI estimators on low- to medium-dimensional datasets, offering a clear trade-off between structural assumptions and computational efficiency. It serves as an excellent case study in how domain-specific statistical frameworks can provide more transparent and faster alternatives to black-box deep learning models.
explanations.expert: VINE is a non-parametric mutual information (MI) estimator that approximates the joint density via simplified D-vine copulas. By exploiting the structural properties of D-vines, the density ratio is decomposed into a product of pair-copulas, enabling efficient estimation without gradient-based optimization. This contrasts with state-of-the-art neural estimators (e.g., MINE, NWJ) that require training high-capacity neural networks to approximate the density ratio. The authors evaluate VINE against these neural baselines across various regimes, showing that VINE maintains competitive accuracy in low- to medium-dimensional spaces while significantly reducing computational latency. The methodology is particularly effective where the D-vine structure captures the underlying dependency patterns. Limitations are inherent to the simplified D-vine assumption, which may bias results in high-dimensional or highly non-linear settings where the simplification is not well-supported by the underlying data distribution. This work provides a computationally efficient alternative for practitioners who need reliable MI estimates without the convergence challenges or training times associated with deep estimation architectures.

papers.title: Safin-1.5: Safety-Native Architecture and Verifiable Reasoning for Recursive Safety Improvement
papers.abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) enables large language models to advance their capabilities through successive updates, but these updates can also introduce new risks and weaken existing safeguards. In line with the AI-45° Law, we pursue Safety RSI, in which safety develops as an intrinsic capability alongside general model capabilities through continual risk discovery and repair, while preserving utility and limiting over-refusal. We introduce Safin-1.5, a model built on a safety architecture and trained through recursive safety improvement, with an inference-time harness that extends its capabilities to formal reasoning. Our approach comprises three components: i) The safety architecture combines persistent safety states with hazardous-knowledge disentanglement. The former retains and selectively invokes safety knowledge, while the latter relocates targeted hazardous knowledge into removable experts, enabling its removal with minimal impact on general capabilities. ii) Recursive safety improvement establishes a discovery-evaluation-repair loop. The loop identifies new vulnerabilities and uses experimental feedback to develop repair strategies. It accepts updates only when they improve safety while preserving general capabilities and limiting over-refusal. iii) The formal reasoning harness combines the model's language understanding with symbolic inference and verification. Proof-obligation-guided semantic bridging recovers missing relations in formal representations, enabling symbolic solvers to construct checkable proofs under formalized premises and accepted semantic bridges. Experimental results demonstrate that Safin-1.5 achieves safety and reasoning performance, outperforming frontier models.
papers.what_changed: Safin-1.5 introduces a safety-native architecture featuring persistent safety states and hazardous-knowledge disentanglement, alongside a recursive safety improvement loop and a formal reasoning inference-time harness.
papers.why_it_matters: It offers a path to build AI systems that can improve their own safety capabilities recursively without degrading performance, addressing a critical bottleneck in the long-term safety of advanced AI models.

explanations.plain: As AI models get smarter, they risk becoming dangerous or learning bad habits. Safin-1.5 is a new approach designed to let an AI improve itself while keeping safety at the forefront. Imagine a student who is constantly studying to get better at math, but every time they learn a new concept, they also take a mandatory class on ethics to ensure they use their skills responsibly. Safin-1.5 does something similar by separating 'dangerous knowledge' into a specific box that can be removed if needed, and by using a verification tool to double-check its reasoning. This helps the AI get more capable at problem-solving without becoming reckless or forgetting the safety rules it was taught at the start.
explanations.student: Safin-1.5 addresses the challenges of Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI), where models update themselves but risk catastrophic forgetting of safety alignment. The core contribution is a three-part architecture. First, a safety-native design uses persistent safety states and hazardous-knowledge disentanglement, which effectively separates harmful information into removable expert modules, preventing performance degradation when safety updates occur. Second, it employs a discovery-evaluation-repair loop. This iterative process acts as a continuous quality control mechanism, accepting model updates only if they satisfy specific safety benchmarks while maintaining utility and avoiding over-refusal. Third, the formal reasoning harness introduces a layer of symbolic verification. It uses proof-obligation-guided semantic bridging, which links the model's natural language understanding with formal symbolic solvers. By translating queries into a logic-based representation, the model can generate checkable proofs, reducing hallucinations in reasoning-heavy tasks. This systematic approach ensures that as the model advances its general capabilities, its safety protocols and reasoning accuracy scale proportionally, rather than decaying through successive cycles of self-improvement.
explanations.expert: Safin-1.5 proposes a framework for Safety Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI) aligned with the AI-45° Law, focusing on concurrent advancement of model utility and safety. The architecture implements three key modules: 1) Persistent safety states and hazardous-knowledge disentanglement; this isolates dangerous parameters into specialized expert components, allowing for pruning or modification without damaging broader latent representations. 2) A recursive improvement pipeline (discovery-evaluation-repair) that treats safety as an intrinsic capability, utilizing experimental feedback to validate updates against safety-utility trade-offs. 3) A formal reasoning harness that leverages proof-obligation-guided semantic bridging to interface language models with symbolic solvers. This allows for the generation of verifiable proofs from formalized premises, effectively mitigating reliance on purely probabilistic reasoning. The paper reports that Safin-1.5 outperforms existing frontier models on composite benchmarks involving both safety-critical tasks and formal reasoning capabilities. Limitations primarily concern the scalability of formalization for open-ended domains and the computational overhead introduced by the inference-time verification harness.

papers.title: Training Foundation Models with a Single Algorithm
papers.abstract: Foundation models are typically trained in stages: pretraining, midtraining, supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and reinforcement learning (RL), with changes in both data and learning algorithms. We show that this algorithmic separation is not fundamental. By deriving suitable RL objectives as maximum-likelihood fitting to model-generated target distributions, we place all of these stages under a single likelihood-based training algorithm, unified training. This perspective turns the foundation-model training lifecycle into a problem of choosing which data to train on, in what proportions, and when, with conventional staged training as a special case. We instantiate this framework in a unified training system that mixes static data and RL generations within a single trainer. Across controlled and real-world experiments, unified training improves the accuracy-compute tradeoff and task coverage while preserving broader capabilities, and provides a stronger starting point for continual learning. This work lays the groundwork for a unified science of foundation-model training, connecting mathematical principles, training infrastructure, and the development of model capabilities.
papers.what_changed: The authors introduce a 'unified training' framework that replaces the traditional staged pipeline (pretraining, SFT, and RL) with a single likelihood-based algorithm. They achieve this by deriving RL objectives as maximum-likelihood fitting to target distributions generated by the model.
papers.why_it_matters: Researchers and practitioners should care because this method simplifies the complex, multi-stage training pipelines for large models into a single, cohesive workflow, potentially leading to more efficient training and better model performance.

explanations.plain: Building a large AI model usually feels like a relay race where different teams use completely different sets of rules at each stage. One team handles the initial learning, another handles specialized instructions, and a third handles behavioral feedback. This paper suggests that we do not actually need these separate rulebooks. Instead, they propose a 'unified training' method that uses a single mathematical approach to handle all stages at once. Imagine learning to play a musical instrument by having three different teachers with conflicting styles, versus having one teacher who uses a single, consistent method for every phase of your growth. By treating the entire process as one continuous task, this approach makes training more efficient and helps the model retain its skills better as it grows.
explanations.student: The current standard for training foundation models involves a disjointed pipeline: pretraining, midtraining, supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and reinforcement learning (RL) from human feedback. Each stage often utilizes distinct loss functions and training regimes, which can lead to catastrophic forgetting or sub-optimal knowledge transfer. This paper challenges this paradigm by framing the entire training lifecycle through a unified likelihood-based objective. The core idea is to express reinforcement learning objectives as maximum-likelihood estimation (MLE) problems, where the model learns to fit target distributions it generates itself. By treating RL as a distribution-matching problem, the researchers integrate static datasets and policy-generated samples into a single training loop. This transforms the training process into a decision problem regarding data sampling proportions and scheduling rather than algorithmic switching. Consequently, the researchers demonstrate that staged training is merely a special case of this broader unified framework. This approach improves the accuracy-compute tradeoff, meaning the models reach higher performance thresholds using fewer resources, while also mitigating issues commonly associated with multi-stage transitions, such as the degradation of base capabilities during fine-tuning. This work suggests that we can optimize the entire foundation model development lifecycle under a consistent mathematical umbrella.
explanations.expert: Traditional LLM training pipelines are notoriously fragmented, requiring distinct optimization strategies for pretraining and RLHF. The authors propose 'Unified Training,' an approach that unifies these stages under a singular likelihood-based objective. By reformulating RL objectives, specifically those involving policy optimization, as maximum-likelihood fitting to model-generated target distributions, the method enables the training of foundation models using a single unified trainer. The framework effectively blends static pretraining data and model-generated RL samples, treating the training trajectory as a continuous optimization problem defined by data mixing schedules. Empirical results demonstrate an improved accuracy-compute tradeoff compared to standard multi-stage pipelines. Furthermore, the framework preserves generalist capabilities while providing a more stable foundation for continual learning, effectively eliminating the algorithmic divergence typically seen between pretraining and subsequent alignment phases. The authors frame standard staged training as a degenerate case within this broader unified framework, where the mixture of data distributions is gated by time. Limitations are not explicitly quantified in the abstract, but the methodology implies a dependency on the quality of model-generated target distributions and the potential complexity of balancing the gradient signals from diverse data sources within a single training loop.

papers.title: EnvOS: Auditing Computer-Use Agents When the World Moves On : Phenomenon-Based Task Construction, Certification, and Evidence-Based Evaluation
papers.abstract: Computer-use agents built on large language models (LLMs) work in software that can change while they act: an appointment moves, a policy is revised, a record is updated. Testing agents under such changes is harder than it looks. When an agent fails, the cause may be the agent, but it may also be a change that did not fire as intended, an update the agent never received, or a grader that scored the episode wrongly. We introduce EnvOS, a framework for building and certifying environments that change mid-task. Before any agent runs, EnvOS checks that each change fires correctly, that the task remains solvable, and that the grader separates correct from incorrect behavior; after each run, separate code re-checks the verdict from archived evidence. We apply it to stale information, where a value the agent has already seen changes before the agent acts on it. In clinic booking, Claude Opus 5 succeeds on 0/16 tasks when nothing extra is shown, 2/16 when reminded to re-check the source, and 15/16 when the updated value is shown; the gain over the reminder holds after correcting for all tests (p = 0.00293). In insurance-claim approval, Opus 5 re-checks on its own and succeeds on 10/10, whereas Claude Sonnet 5 rises from 1/10 to 9/10 when the current policy is shown again, a gain significant in its pre-registered test but not after correcting for all tests. Whether an agent caught a change thus varied with the model and the interface. We also stress-test the grading itself: on corrupted episodes designed blind from the rules, the EnvOS pipeline accepted none of 26 as clean, and on an externally generated set it caught 25 of 39, against 4 for simple log checks. Because every EnvOS environment is generated from a seed and graded by an audited automatic verifier, the same environments are natural candidates for training agents with reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards.
papers.what_changed: The authors introduce EnvOS, a framework that audits computer-use agents by certifying that dynamic task environments work correctly and that grading logic is robust to mid-task updates.
papers.why_it_matters: As agents move from static benchmarks to real-world software, their ability to handle shifting information is critical. Researchers and developers need this framework to ensure agent failures are due to the agent's reasoning rather than flawed testing environments.

explanations.plain: Imagine you are taking a math test, but while you are working, the teacher changes the numbers in the problems without telling you. If you get the answer wrong, is it because you do not know math, or because the test was unfair? Computer-use agents face this exact problem when they work in real-world software. EnvOS is a new system designed to make sure these "test" environments are fair. It checks the environment before the agent starts to make sure the problems can actually be solved. It also acts like a strict auditor, verifying that the agent's score is accurate even when the information changes halfway through. It prevents the testing process itself from being the reason an agent fails.
explanations.student: Computer-use agents based on Large Language Models (LLMs) operate in dynamic environments where underlying states may change mid-task. Testing these agents is difficult because it is often unclear if a failure stems from model limitations, environment instability, or flawed grading. EnvOS is a framework that introduces a rigorous pipeline for environment certification and evidence-based evaluation. It ensures task solvability and validator reliability by pre-verifying state changes and post-verifying verdicts against archived logs. The authors demonstrate this by testing models like Claude Opus 5 and Claude Sonnet 5 on clinic booking and insurance tasks with changing data. They show that performance is highly dependent on whether the model is prompted or shown updated values. Crucially, EnvOS also stress-tests the graders themselves against corrupted episodes to ensure they correctly reject invalid data. By using seed-based environment generation and audited verifiers, the framework provides a foundation for training agents using reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, addressing the 'garbage in, garbage out' problem in agent evaluation.
explanations.expert: EnvOS addresses the challenge of evaluating autonomous computer-use agents in non-static, stochastic environments. The framework formalizes the lifecycle of an agent-environment interaction: pre-run verification of task feasibility and change triggers, and post-run audit of evaluation logic using archived state traces. The authors evaluate this on two domains: clinic booking and insurance-claim approval. In clinic booking, Claude Opus 5 improved from 0/16 to 15/16 success rate when updated values were provided, with a statistically significant gain (p=0.00293). In insurance-claim tasks, Claude Sonnet 5 improved from 1/10 to 9/10, though significance vanished after multiple-testing correction. A core contribution is the stress-testing of the grading infrastructure itself; EnvOS correctly rejected all 26 corrupted episodes, and captured 25/39 externally generated corrupted tasks compared to 4/39 for standard log-based checks. Limitations include model-specific sensitivity to UI updates and the necessity of domain-specific auditing for every new environment. By guaranteeing that every environment is generated from a reproducible seed and accompanied by an audited verifier, EnvOS facilitates the transition from static benchmarks to verifiable reinforcement learning environments.

papers.title: Proving and Improving the Platonic Representation Hypothesis with JEPAs
papers.abstract: Whether models trained on different modalities converge to the same representation of the world is central to AI. The Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH) conjectures that they do as they scale, but without a proof it offers neither a guarantee nor a recipe. We turn the hypothesis into a theorem. First, we prove a \emph{Platonic Representation Theorem}: Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) trained separately on any number of modalities learn the same representation up to one rotation whenever their positive pairs are two observations of one scene--\emph{good views}--and their misalignment is bounded otherwise. Second, we show that next-token prediction is a JEPA with \emph{bad views}, parts of a single document, which explains why language models align with vision only through scale. Third, we validate the theory from 145k captions to the texts of 940M web images, and uncover a scaling law of alignment that predicts unseen runs within seed noise. Good views need 42 times fewer training samples than next-token prediction on the same corpus to reach the same alignment, and a 109M-parameter text JEPA aligns with DINOv2 and CLIP's image encoders better than every language model we evaluated, up to 72B parameters, and than CLIP's text encoder: next-token prediction is a remarkably inefficient route to platonic representations. As a showcase, one rotation turns separately trained encoders into an image captioner (CIDEr .838 on COCO). Even that rotation needs no pair: on the latest pair-free benchmark, our text JEPA beats every zero-shot accuracy reported with language models up to 8B parameters, e.g., 64\% against at most 56\% top-5 on ImageNet-100. Positive views, and not scale alone, are thus the lever to build platonic representations.
papers.what_changed: The authors prove a Platonic Representation Theorem for Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) and demonstrate that JEPAs achieve better cross-modal alignment than next-token prediction models using 42 times fewer training samples.
papers.why_it_matters: This research provides a theoretical foundation for how AI models can converge on a shared understanding of the world, suggesting that smarter training objectives, rather than just massive scale, are key to building efficient, unified AI systems.

explanations.plain: Imagine you and a friend are trying to learn what a 'dog' is. You look at pictures, while your friend reads descriptions. If you both learn well, you should eventually end up with a very similar concept of a dog in your minds, even though you used different sources. This paper explores the idea that AI models, like those for images and text, might converge on the same 'platonic' understanding of the world. The authors prove that using a specific architecture called JEPA helps models arrive at this shared understanding much faster than current methods. Think of it like using a highly efficient study guide instead of reading a whole library; they show that choosing the right training data is far more important than just making models bigger.
explanations.student: The Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH) suggests that models trained on different modalities eventually converge to identical internal representations. The authors formalize this by proving the Platonic Representation Theorem for Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs). A JEPA learns by predicting missing parts of a scene from other views, which the authors identify as 'good views.' In contrast, next-token prediction, the standard for Large Language Models, uses 'bad views' (fragments of a single text stream), leading to inefficient alignment. The paper demonstrates that JEPA encoders can achieve stronger cross-modal alignment with fewer samples than next-token prediction architectures. For instance, a 109M-parameter JEPA outperforms 72B-parameter language models in aligning with established vision encoders like DINOv2. This suggests that the objective function and the nature of the data pairs are critical, challenging the assumption that massive scale is the only path to universal representation alignment. The practical implication is a new, lightweight way to create cross-modal systems: by training encoders separately and applying a simple rotation, they achieve high-quality zero-shot performance on benchmarks like ImageNet-100 without needing massive-scale joint training.
explanations.expert: The authors formalize the Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH) via a new theorem proving that JEPAs (Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures) trained on 'good views' (spatially or temporally related observations of the same scene) converge to identical representations up to a rotation. They classify next-token prediction as a sub-optimal objective due to 'bad views' (token sequences within a single document). Empirical validation shows that JEPAs require 42x fewer training samples to reach comparable alignment to autoregressive models. A 109M-parameter text JEPA demonstrated superior alignment with DINOv2 and CLIP image encoders compared to language models up to 72B parameters. Furthermore, the approach achieved zero-shot ImageNet-100 accuracy of 64% (top-5), outperforming baseline models of up to 8B parameters. The findings establish a scaling law for alignment and demonstrate that simple rotations can enable zero-shot cross-modal tasks, such as image captioning (CIDEr 0.838 on COCO). The results suggest that the bottleneck for cross-modal convergence is the training objective's ability to provide high-quality positive views, rather than the raw model parameter count.

papers.title: Let LiDAR Decide Where to Look: Geometry-Measured Token Selection for Efficient Sparse Latent World Models
papers.abstract: Vision-centric autonomous driving models encode thousands of image tokens per frame, yet most depict sky, buildings, or empty road---content irrelevant to planning. Worse, these tokens dilute the planner's attention: we show that randomly discarding 75% of tokens already outperforms the dense model, because the planner can concentrate on the remaining driving-critical content. Building on this finding, we present Geometry-Aware Token Selection (GATS), which uses LiDAR and radar point projections to select a small fraction of image tokens before the vision backbone runs. Because the selector operates on measured 3D geometry rather than visual features, the backbone encodes only the selected patches, cutting end-to-end FLOPs by up to $18\times$. Each kept token receives a 3D anchor from its LiDAR point and is fed to a self-supervised latent world model that predicts future features and 3D displacements without box annotations. At 25% budget, GATS achieves a 3-sec L2 displacement error of 0.520 m on nuScenes and an EPDMS of 88.9 on NAVSIM---surpassing the dense baseline (0.573 m / 85.9) at $6.6\times$ fewer total FLOPs. At an extreme 10% budget (24 GFLOPs, $18\times$ reduction), it still beats the dense baseline on both nuScenes (0.537 m vs. 0.573 m L2) and NAVSIM (87.9 vs. 85.9 EPDMS). On 739 intent-critical scenarios, GATS covers 95.8% of hazardous vehicles and achieves a 0.09% collision rate---73.5% lower than the dense model (0.34%).
papers.what_changed: The authors introduce Geometry-Aware Token Selection (GATS), a method that uses LiDAR and radar data to pre-select relevant image patches before vision processing, reducing FLOPs by up to 18x.
papers.why_it_matters: It demonstrates that discarding irrelevant visual data allows autonomous driving models to plan more accurately while using significantly less computational power.

explanations.plain: Modern self-driving cars process huge amounts of visual data, but much of it is useless, like pictures of the sky or empty walls. This paper introduces a smart filter that uses lasers to look at the world first. By measuring distance with lasers, the car identifies exactly which parts of a camera image are important for driving and ignores the rest. Think of it like a human driver using peripheral vision to ignore clouds while focusing intently on the road ahead. By ignoring the clutter, the car's computer can think much faster and make safer decisions. The result is a system that uses far less energy while actually performing better at predicting hazards than systems that try to look at everything at once.
explanations.student: The paper tackles the challenge of computational inefficiency in vision-centric autonomous driving, where dense image encoding processes many irrelevant tokens. The authors observe that random token discarding outperforms dense models, suggesting that reducing input density improves planner focus. They propose Geometry-Aware Token Selection (GATS), a pre-processing method that uses 3D point cloud projections from LiDAR and radar sensors to filter image patches. Only selected patches are passed to the vision backbone, which feeds into a self-supervised latent world model that predicts future displacements without needing manual 3D bounding box annotations. By prioritizing geometry over visual features, the system achieves a 18x reduction in Floating Point Operations (FLOPs). Performance metrics show significant improvements over dense baselines: on the nuScenes dataset, GATS achieves an L2 displacement error of 0.520m at 25% budget, compared to 0.573m for the dense model. Furthermore, the model shows improved safety in intent-critical scenarios, with a 73.5% reduction in collision rates. This highlights how leveraging sparse, geometry-based priors can optimize latent world models for real-time robotic applications.
explanations.expert: GATS addresses the redundancy in vision-centric autonomous driving pipelines by introducing a LiDAR-guided token selection mechanism.
