PRISM resolves this by introducing an iterative proximal refinement scheme. It constructs an objective-aware proximal distribution $p(x | x_k)$ conditioned on the current iterate $x_k$. This stochastic framework recovers the convergence properties of Riemannian gradient descent without requiring explicit tangent space projections. The authors establish theoretical guarantees for the descent property, feasibility (adherence to the support of the manifold distribution), and convergence to first-order stationarity. Empirical validation includes synthetic geometric tasks and data-driven building control. Limitations include the reliance on the quality of the sampled proximal distribution and the density of feasible samples in the region of interest. By removing the requirement for explicit manifold definitions, PRISM generalizes optimization to complex, data-defined sets common in high-dimensional engineering applications.

papers.title: Follow the Features: SAE Feature-Guided Data-Efficient Instruction-Tuning of Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Selecting small, effective instruction-tuning datasets requires identifying which aspects of the original data to retain. We introduce Follow the Features (FtF), a data-selection method that uses sparse autoencoder (SAE) features to characterize training data and guide subset construction. FtF ranks features using dataset-level activation statistics, scores samples by their expression of highly ranked features, and incorporates feature resampling to encourage diversity. The LLM-SAE pair used for selection is independent of the model being fine-tuned, enabling reuse across target models. We evaluate FtF on two model-dataset settings at a training budget of 100 samples with a fixed sequence length of 256 tokens. FtF achieves performance competitive with GRAPE and S2L, with relative rankings varying across settings. On Qwen 3 8B trained on Alpaca, FtF exceeds full-dataset training by 1.59 percentage points in the harmonic mean of an AlpacaEval-based win rate and Open LLM Leaderboard performance, although full-dataset training retains a higher Leaderboard score. These results support SAE feature statistics as a useful signal for data-efficient instruction tuning.
papers.what_changed: The authors introduce Follow the Features (FtF), a data-selection method that uses sparse autoencoder (SAE) feature activation statistics to rank and select training samples, including a resampling step to ensure diversity.
papers.why_it_matters: This research provides a way to train high-performing LLMs on significantly smaller, curated subsets of data, which reduces computational costs and data management overhead.

explanations.plain: Training large language models requires massive amounts of data, which is expensive and time-consuming. This paper introduces a technique called Follow the Features (FtF) to pick only the most important parts of a dataset. Imagine you are trying to learn a new language. Instead of reading the entire library, you would want to pick the most informative books that cover the widest range of grammar and vocabulary. FtF acts like a librarian that uses 'sparse autoencoders', a tool that acts like an X-ray for AI brains, to see which specific patterns, or features, are hidden inside the data. By picking samples that contain these high-quality patterns, the AI can learn effectively with much less data.
explanations.student: Data-efficient instruction tuning focuses on subset selection: picking a small number of prompts that maximize model performance. The authors present Follow the Features (FtF), which leverages Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to represent training data. An SAE learns a dictionary of features from the internal activations of a model. FtF works by calculating dataset-level activation statistics for these SAE features to determine their importance. It then scores samples based on how strongly they activate these 'top' features while employing a resampling technique to ensure diversity in the subset. A key advantage of FtF is that the SAE used to extract these features can be decoupled from the target model, making the method portable. The researchers evaluated FtF on Qwen 3 8B using 100 samples. Results show that FtF is competitive with existing selection methods like GRAPE and S2L. Notably, on the Alpaca dataset, FtF outperformed full-dataset training by 1.59 percentage points in a harmonic mean of AlpacaEval win rates and Open LLM Leaderboard scores, suggesting that SAE-based selection can be an efficient alternative to traditional full-fine-tuning.
explanations.expert: FtF utilizes Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) features as a proxy for information density in instruction-tuning datasets. By computing activation statistics across the dataset, the method identifies highly activated features and uses them to score individual samples. To mitigate redundancy, FtF incorporates a feature resampling step to prioritize diversity during subset construction. A primary architectural benefit is the model-agnostic nature of the selection process; the SAE-LLM pair used for scoring can be independent of the target fine-tuning model. Evaluation was conducted at a strict 100-sample budget with a fixed 256-token sequence length. In the Alpaca-Qwen 3 8B setting, FtF achieved a harmonic mean of AlpacaEval win rate and Open LLM Leaderboard performance that exceeded the full-dataset baseline by 1.59 percentage points. However, the study notes that the full-dataset model maintained a superior absolute Open LLM Leaderboard score, indicating a trade-off between task-specific instruction following and generalized benchmark performance. FtF demonstrates that SAE-based feature signals are a robust alternative to gradient-based selection methods like GRAPE and S2L.

papers.title: Self-Supervised Learning of Universal Latent Spaces for Operator Learning
papers.abstract: Neural operators fit their representation of functions to the task they are trained on, so every new task rebuilds a reduced space from labeled data. Following the self-supervised pre-training that made representations shareable in natural language processing and computer vision, we decouple representation learning from operator learning. A functional autoencoder is pre-trained on analytic functions synthesized on the fly, with no solver and no labels, to represent functions on arbitrary point clouds, and the latent space it induces is frozen and reused across tasks. The representation is exactly equivariant to translation, dilation, and amplitude, and reconstructs solutions of partial differential equations (PDEs) and natural images on geometries it never saw. Being task-agnostic, the latent space can be interpreted in its own right. The whole space is used and decodes to valid fields, it preserves the ordering of distances between physical fields, its geodesics interpolate physical evolutions, and edit directions transfer across fields. With frozen representation maps, a dataset is encoded once and a neural operator is trained entirely on cached embeddings, which saves memory and training time. On 28 tasks in fluid dynamics, solid mechanics, acoustics, and the Helmholtz and Poisson equations, this paradigm can exceed the accuracy of state-of-the-art end-to-end architectures, with up to an order of magnitude higher throughput and memory savings that fit models nearly two orders of magnitude larger on consumer-grade GPUs. At inference, latent rollouts run up to an order of magnitude faster than regular rollouts, and chunked inference processes functions of over half a billion points on a single consumer-grade GPU.
papers.what_changed: The authors introduce a functional autoencoder that decouples representation learning from operator learning, creating a universal, task-agnostic latent space for neural operators. This space is pre-trained via self-supervision on analytic functions and remains frozen, allowing for significantly faster training and inference through cached embeddings.
papers.why_it_matters: Researchers and engineers working on scientific computing and physical simulations should care because this method drastically reduces the computational cost of training neural operators while achieving state-of-the-art accuracy across diverse physical domains.

explanations.plain: Imagine you are trying to learn how to play many different musical instruments. Usually, you would have to start from scratch for every single one. Instead, these researchers created a universal system that learns the basic language of 'sound' first. By training a model on general mathematical patterns without looking at any specific problems, they created a shorthand code. When the model later encounters a difficult task, like simulating how air flows over an airplane wing or how heat spreads through metal, it uses this shorthand instead of learning from scratch. It is like having a master dictionary that allows you to translate any new language instantly. This makes scientific simulations much faster, cheaper to run, and capable of handling massive amounts of data on standard home computers.
explanations.student: In neural operator learning, the typical approach is to learn a mapping between function spaces specifically for a given task, which requires re-training from scratch for every new scenario. This paper introduces a functional autoencoder trained in a self-supervised fashion on synthesized analytic functions, completely independent of labeled task data. The core innovation is that this latent space is frozen and equivariant to transformations like translation, dilation, and amplitude. By encoding inputs into this universal latent space, the subsequent task-specific operator operates entirely on cached embeddings. This architectural decoupling significantly enhances efficiency; the paper reports training and memory throughput improvements of up to an order of magnitude. Crucially, because the representation is task-agnostic, the latent space exhibits desirable geometric properties, such as preserving distances between physical fields and allowing for meaningful interpolation through geodesics. For students, this highlights the growing trend of leveraging self-supervised pre-training to build reusable representations that generalize across domains, extending the success seen in NLP and computer vision into the realm of scientific machine learning and PDE solvers.
explanations.expert: This work introduces a self-supervised functional autoencoder that decouples representation learning from downstream operator learning for PDEs. By pre-training on synthesized analytic functions without ground-truth PDE solvers, the model induces a frozen, task-agnostic latent space. The representation is mathematically rigorous, satisfying equivariance to translation, dilation, and amplitude transformations. By encoding data once into these cached embeddings, the authors demonstrate a paradigm shift in neural operator training: downstream models are trained solely on fixed latent representations, yielding significant computational gains. Empirical results across 28 diverse tasks, including fluid dynamics, solid mechanics, and various elliptic PDEs, show the approach exceeds state-of-the-art end-to-end architectures in accuracy. The hardware efficiency is substantial: it achieves an order of magnitude higher throughput and enables processing of fields with over 500 million points on a single consumer GPU. The latent space demonstrates excellent interpretability, with geodetic properties allowing for smooth interpolation and transferrable edit directions. Limitations are not explicitly detailed, but the reliance on pre-trained analytic functions suggests the quality of the latent space depends on the breadth of the synthetic training manifold.

papers.title: Generative Modeling for Cascading Extremes via Autoregressive Transformers
papers.abstract: Extreme events often occur sequentially, from earthquake-tsunami cascades to successive extreme losses in financial markets. We introduce an extremal token representation that encodes multivariate observations as a categorical sequence. A quiet token records the absence of threshold exceedances; otherwise, the token identifies the exceeding component with the largest marginal probability-scale score. The representation is invariant to componentwise strictly increasing transformations. It preserves the identity and temporal ordering of dominant exceedances but discards their magnitudes and the identities of nondominant simultaneous exceedances. A decoder-only transformer estimates the history-dependent next-token kernel on this representation, and recursive sampling generates future token sequences from the induced joint predictive law. We amortize our generative model by pretraining across simulated process families with varying parameters and dependence persistence. Next-token predictions are evaluated against exact conditional probabilities for held-out categorical processes and particle filter references for heavy-tailed vector autoregressive processes. Applied to ten-second returns for five semiconductor stocks, the pretrained model supports zero-shot transfer, while a few epochs of adaptation improve agreement between observed and generated token frequencies and transition patterns. These results support task-specific tokenization and simulation-based pretraining for modeling which dimensions dominate multivariate extremes.
papers.what_changed: The authors introduce an 'extremal token representation' that converts multivariate extreme events into categorical sequences, which are then modeled by a decoder-only transformer. This allows the system to generate future sequences of extreme event occurrences by learning history-dependent kernels via simulation-based pretraining.
papers.why_it_matters: This approach helps researchers and analysts predict the sequence of extreme events in complex systems, such as financial market crashes or natural disasters, where understanding the timing and identity of the next dominant event is critical.

explanations.plain: Imagine you are tracking weather events. Instead of trying to measure exactly how many inches of rain fall or how fast every wind gust is, you just focus on which specific weather station reports the biggest problem at any given moment. The researchers created a new way to turn these complex, extreme events into a simple string of 'tokens' or labels. Think of this like turning a chaotic, noisy symphony into a simple musical score that only tracks which instrument hits the loudest note next. They then use an AI model similar to those that power chatbots to learn the pattern of these notes. This helps the system predict the likely order of future disasters, even if it cannot predict the exact intensity.
explanations.student: This research addresses the challenge of modeling multivariate extreme events, which are statistically rare but impactful. The authors propose a custom tokenization scheme for extremes: a 'quiet token' represents periods below a threshold, while other tokens encode the index of the component (e.g., a specific stock) showing the most significant exceedance. This representation is invariant to componentwise strictly increasing transformations, meaning it focuses on the ordinal ranking of extremes rather than absolute magnitudes. The core architecture is a decoder-only transformer trained to predict the next token in the sequence based on historical context. To enable zero-shot transfer, the model is pretrained on simulated process families with varying parameters and temporal dependence. This approach effectively treats the problem of predicting multivariate cascades as a discrete sequence generation task. By abstracting away the exact magnitudes and focusing on the identity of the dominant exceeding component, the transformer can capture complex dependencies in heavy-tailed data. The authors validate this against exact conditional probabilities and particle filter benchmarks, demonstrating that the model can be adapted to real-world financial data with minimal fine-tuning.
explanations.expert: The paper introduces an extremal token representation designed to map multivariate observations into categorical sequences suitable for transformer-based generative modeling. The representation preserves the temporal order and identity of the dominant component exceeding a specified threshold while discarding magnitudes and nondominant exceedances. The model utilizes a decoder-only transformer architecture to estimate the history-dependent next-token kernel. Pretraining is conducted via an amortized inference framework using simulated process families with diverse dependence persistence, facilitating zero-shot capability. The authors evaluate the induced joint predictive law against ground-truth conditional probabilities for categorical processes and particle filter estimates for heavy-tailed vector autoregressive processes. In empirical applications involving ten-second semiconductor stock returns, the model demonstrates robust zero-shot performance and effective adaptation after minimal fine-tuning. Limitations inherent in this framework include the loss of magnitude information and the exclusion of nondominant simultaneous exceedances, which may restrict its utility in applications requiring precise quantification of tail risk severity. The method provides a novel intersection between extreme value theory and sequential generative modeling, specifically targeting the prediction of dominant dimensions in multivariate cascades.

papers.title: A Circuit for In-Context Learning
papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) lets a pretrained language model perform a task specified by demonstrations in its prompt, with no parameter updates. With arbitrary labels the model must acquire a mapping it cannot have memorized, so the learning happens within a single forward pass. Prior work found candidate parts but not how they compose. We give the composition for few-shot sentence classification with arbitrary labels in three 3-4B-parameter transformers. The model implements a key-value memory over label-token positions: each label token's residual stream encodes the label's identity, and middle-layer attention heads write into it the class of the preceding demonstration as its key. At the query, upper-layer heads match the query's class against the stored keys and copy out the matching labels. An early-layer signal encoding whether any label has repeated gates this readout; in its absence the readers attend to the start of the prompt and no label is favored. A separate set of heads suppresses the most recently seen label. Each step is established causally by activation patching, head ablations against random-head baselines, and steering with the model's own signals. A softmax model of the readout with two constants per head, fit on one prompt distribution, predicts another. The computation is conserved across the three models, the named heads alone reproduce the behaviour, and a transformer trained from scratch grows the same parts. The circuit transfers to semantic concepts and to labels with meaning, and the same parts, with a causal gate, appear from 0.6B to 8B in one family and survive instruction tuning. ICL in this setting is a gated associative lookup built from a few identifiable component types, traced causally from demonstrations to prediction.
papers.what_changed: The authors identify a specific neural circuit consisting of key-value memory heads and gating mechanisms that enables few-shot sentence classification in 3-4B parameter transformers. They demonstrate that these models perform in-context learning by storing demonstration labels as keys and retrieving them during the query phase through a gated associative lookup mechanism.
papers.why_it_matters: This research provides a concrete, mechanistic explanation for how transformers perform tasks without parameter updates. It helps practitioners understand the internal logic of language models and provides a blueprint for how learning behavior emerges from architectural components.

explanations.plain: Large language models can learn new tasks simply by reading a few examples in a prompt, a process called in-context learning. We usually treat this like a black box, but this paper looks inside to see how the model actually does it. Think of it like a librarian helping a student who has never seen a specific textbook before. The model reads the examples provided at the beginning, remembers which labels belong to which sentences, and then applies that logic when it reaches the final question. The researchers discovered that the model uses specific groups of 'neurons' to act like a filing system, creating a key-value record of the examples and then matching the final question against that record to find the right answer.
explanations.student: In-context learning (ICL) refers to the ability of frozen pretrained transformers to adapt to new tasks via few-shot prompts. This paper employs mechanistic interpretability to reverse-engineer the specific circuit responsible for ICL in 3-4B parameter models. The researchers identify a gated associative lookup mechanism. In this setup, attention heads in middle layers function as a key-value memory, writing the class label of preceding demonstrations into the residual stream. Subsequent query-time attention heads retrieve these labels by matching the query's classification features against the stored keys. The authors establish this via activation patching and head ablations, showing that the circuit is causal and conserved across model sizes (0.6B to 8B parameters). They specifically observe an early-layer gating signal that detects label repetition, which controls whether the model favors the prompt-derived labels or defaults to a neutral state. This shows that ICL is not emergent magic but the result of identifiable, modular circuits that function as a targeted memory store.
explanations.expert: This study performs a causal deconstruction of in-context learning (ICL) in 3-4B parameter transformers, identifying a distinct circuit for few-shot sentence classification with arbitrary labels. The architecture implements a gated associative lookup where middle-layer attention heads operate as write heads for a key-value store, encoding class identity into the residual stream at demonstration positions. At the query position, upper-layer heads perform retrieval by matching query class features against stored keys. A crucial gating signal in early layers, triggered by label repetition, modulates this readout; absent this signal, the model reverts to attending to the prompt's beginning. Causal evidence is provided through activation patching and head ablations, showing that these specific subgraphs are sufficient to replicate the ICL behavior. The model performance is validated using a softmax readout model with two learned constants per head, which generalizes across prompt distributions. Furthermore, the researchers observe that this circuit is conserved across the 0.6B to 8B parameter range and persists through instruction tuning. The finding confirms that ICL in this configuration is a mechanistically grounded associative lookup, offering a clear causal trace from demonstration inputs to final prediction output.

papers.title: Neural networks and games
papers.abstract: Hopfield neural networks and noncooperative games provide seemingly different approaches to understanding how collective outcomes emerge from local interactions. In a neural network, individual units adjust their states according to local signals; in a game, players choose actions to maximise individual payoffs. I establish an exact equivalence between symmetric binary Hopfield networks and binary-action games that admit a quadratic potential. The equivalence identifies stable network configurations with pure-strategy Nash equilibria, and asynchronous neural updating with best-response dynamics. More broadly, the storage and retrieval of memories in neural networks correspond, respectively, to the design and selection of equilibria in games.
papers.what_changed: The paper establishes an exact mathematical equivalence between symmetric binary Hopfield neural networks and binary-action games that admit a quadratic potential.
papers.why_it_matters: This connection allows researchers to translate tools and insights between neuroscience and economics, specifically linking memory retrieval in neural networks to equilibrium selection in game theory.

explanations.plain: Imagine two different groups trying to solve a puzzle. One group is made of tiny electronic brain cells in a computer, while the other is a group of competitive people playing a game. This research shows that these two activities are actually the same thing in disguise. A computer adjusting its settings to remember something is mathematically identical to a group of players settling on a final decision in a game. Think of it like learning that a recipe for baking bread and a formula for building a skyscraper use the exact same logic. By proving this link, scientists can now use the rules of games to understand how computers think, or use the math of brain networks to better predict human behavior in competitive situations.
explanations.student: The paper demonstrates an isomorphism between symmetric binary Hopfield networks and a specific class of noncooperative games known as potential games. A Hopfield network consists of binary units that update their states based on local energy minimization. In game theory, potential games are those where the incentives of all players can be expressed by a single global function, the potential function. The author shows that the stable configurations of a Hopfield network map directly to pure-strategy Nash equilibria. Furthermore, the process of asynchronous neural updating, where units change state to lower local energy, is mathematically equivalent to best-response dynamics in games, where players change actions to increase their individual payoffs. This bridge allows us to view memory storage in neural networks as the process of designing equilibria in economic systems. By identifying these parallels, the study provides a formal framework for applying game-theoretic analysis to collective emergent behaviors in neural architectures. It simplifies complex neural dynamics by recontextualizing them through the lens of strategic interaction, potentially offering new ways to interpret how networks converge toward stable states by leveraging the existing literature on equilibrium selection and convergence rates in game-theoretic models.
explanations.expert: This paper presents a formal mapping between symmetric binary Hopfield networks and binary-action potential games. By identifying the Hamiltonian of the Hopfield network with the negative of the potential function in a game, the author establishes that the energy minimization landscape of the neural network is isomorphic to the payoff structure of a quadratic potential game. Specifically, the local stability of network configurations corresponds to pure-strategy Nash equilibria, while the asynchronous update rule of the neural units is equivalent to the best-response dynamics of the players. The analysis extends this to state transitions, showing that memory retrieval is conceptually linked to equilibrium selection. The primary result is a theoretical synthesis showing that the emergence of stable outcomes in both domains is governed by the same optimization mechanics. The model relies on the symmetry of the weight matrix and the binary nature of the state space, which restricts the equivalence to specific network topologies. The author concludes that the design of memory-based neural systems is effectively an exercise in game design, where the weights of the network represent player payoffs and memory states represent desired stable equilibria. This abstraction provides a rigorous basis for analyzing neural convergence through the convergence properties of game-theoretic learning dynamics.

papers.title: Give the Drafter a Second Chance to Guess: Parallel Reconsideration for Speculative Decoding
papers.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates large language model inference with a small drafter, whose per-guess acceptance rate determines the achievable speedup. Feature-level drafters share a design choice: every token, easy or hard, is drafted under a single forward pass. Many of the tokens the target rejects are ones the drafter is itself unsure about yet the target answers decisively. To address this, we introduce Parallel Reconsideration: guided by its own uncertainty, the drafter reconsiders its hesitant guesses with extra passes that run in parallel with the one-pass draft, adding negligible latency. A co-designed training recipe and serving-time drafting algorithm append these reconsidered guesses to the original draft tree as refined candidates. Across models and benchmarks, on average, Parallel Reconsideration improves over the baselines by 5.3% to 10.2% on acceptance length and by 3.5% to 9.2% on speedup.
papers.what_changed: The authors introduce Parallel Reconsideration, a method that allows a speculative drafter to use additional, parallel forward passes to refine uncertain tokens before the target model checks them.
papers.why_it_matters: It improves the inference efficiency of large language models by increasing the number of tokens accepted per speculative draft, resulting in faster text generation.

explanations.plain: Large language models generate text one word at a time, which can be slow. To speed this up, a small 'drafter' model tries to guess several words at once, which a larger model then quickly checks. Usually, this drafter only gets one chance to guess. The authors found that when the drafter is unsure, it often makes mistakes that the larger model rejects. This paper introduces a method called Parallel Reconsideration. Think of it like a student taking a test who is allowed to double-check their most difficult answers before handing the paper in. By using a little extra computing power to rethink uncertain guesses at the same time, the system gets more words right, making the whole process faster for the user.
explanations.student: Speculative decoding is a popular technique for accelerating Large Language Model (LLM) inference. It uses a lightweight 'draft' model to propose a sequence of tokens, which a larger target model verifies in a single forward pass. The bottleneck is the drafter's accuracy; if the target model rejects the draft, the speedup is negated. Current drafters are constrained to a single forward pass per draft tree. The authors propose Parallel Reconsideration, which allows the drafter to identify hesitant guesses based on its own uncertainty and perform additional forward passes in parallel. These refined candidates are then appended to the draft tree. Because these passes happen concurrently with the initial draft, the latency overhead is minimal. By improving the acceptance rate of the proposed tokens, the model achieves better throughput. Empirically, the method increases the average acceptance length by 5.3% to 10.2% and overall speedup by 3.5% to 9.2% across evaluated benchmarks. The work includes a co-designed training recipe to calibrate the drafter for this reconsideration process, ensuring the model better identifies which tokens require refinement.
explanations.expert: The paper addresses the efficiency limitations of speculative decoding, where the speedup factor is directly tied to the acceptance rate of a draft model. The authors observe that standard drafters generate drafts via a single forward pass, regardless of the inherent uncertainty of specific token predictions. Parallel Reconsideration introduces a mechanism where the drafter evaluates its own uncertainty and triggers parallel inference passes to refine tokens for which it lacks confidence. These 'reconsidered' tokens are structured as an expanded draft tree. The method is supported by a specific training objective that encourages the drafter to produce high-quality alternatives for uncertain slots. Experimental results demonstrate a robust improvement in inference latency: average acceptance length increases by 5.3% to 10.2%, resulting in a 3.5% to 9.2% speedup over baseline speculative decoding. The approach effectively exploits idle parallel capacity to reduce the rejection frequency of the target model. Limitations are not explicitly detailed, but the method assumes the existence of spare computational budget to run the auxiliary forward passes without significantly increasing the wall-clock time of the drafting phase.

papers.title: ViBench 2.0: A Benchmark for Long-Horizon Software Building
papers.abstract: On Replit, our agentic engineering platform, users now build entire products without writing code, through successive feature requests to an agent. Yet existing coding benchmarks evaluate single, fully specified tasks, and many are near saturation. We introduce ViBench 2.0, a benchmark for long-horizon software building that we use to select our platform's models. Its 17 full-stack web products, modeled on widely used software, grow over 241 feature requests and are judged only when finished, as a user would judge them: a browser agent runs 544 test plans, and a build passes only if every plan does, under a grading protocol validated to keep this strict score reliable. Evaluating nine models, we find a reliability gap: the three strongest pass up to 98% of test plans yet deliver a fully working product in at most 65% of builds, and no open-weight model delivers one. The gap is closing fast: across three releases of one model family, pass@1 on the public products rises from 3% to 53% while the cost per build falls by more than half. We release eight products with the harness and grader, hold out nine, and report lessons from production use.
papers.what_changed: ViBench 2.0 introduces a long-horizon benchmark for full-stack software development, evaluating agents on 17 web products requiring 241 consecutive feature requests rather than single-task completion.
papers.why_it_matters: It exposes a reliability gap where AI agents may pass individual test cases but fail to deliver functional software, providing a more realistic metric for real-world engineering platforms.

explanations.plain: Modern AI can write small snippets of code well, but building an entire software application is a long, complicated process. Think of it like the difference between a student answering a single multiple-choice question and a student writing a full novel. If you focus only on the small questions, you might miss if the student can actually string a plot together over hundreds of pages. ViBench 2.0 acts like a final exam that forces an AI to build a complete product from scratch, step by step. It checks if the final result actually works as a user expects, rather than just grading individual lines of code. This helps developers understand if their AI is truly ready to build apps or just guessing at fragments.
explanations.student: ViBench 2.0 addresses a critical limitation in current code-generation evaluation: the reliance on single-turn, isolated function-completion tasks. While existing benchmarks (e.g., HumanEval) measure algorithmic correctness, they fail to account for long-horizon planning and state maintenance in full-stack engineering. The benchmark consists of 17 full-stack web products, requiring a sequence of 241 feature requests. The evaluation protocol uses a browser agent to execute 544 test plans, requiring all plans to pass for a successful build. This represents a significant shift from static unit testing to end-to-end functional validation. The study reveals a 'reliability gap' where even models with high individual test pass rates often fail to produce a functional application. For students, this highlights the discrepancy between model performance on narrow benchmarks versus systemic software engineering, where architectural consistency and long-term context retention are paramount. The authors also demonstrate rapid improvements in model efficiency and success rates across model family releases, illustrating the trend of closing the gap through iterative refinement.
explanations.expert: ViBench 2.0 proposes a benchmark for multi-turn, long-horizon software engineering, shifting away from standard single-function completion tasks toward end-to-end product synthesis. The dataset comprises 17 full-stack web applications, evaluated through 241 sequential feature requests and validated via 544 automated test plans run by a browser agent. A build is defined as successful only if it satisfies all test plans, enforcing strict functional requirements. Empirical results across nine models reveal a significant reliability gap: top models achieving up to 98% pass rates on individual test plans only reach 65% success in delivering functional full-stack products. Notably, no open-weight models currently deliver a fully working product in this environment. The paper also tracks performance gains across a single model family, noting a pass@1 improvement from 3% to 53% while reducing compute cost per build by over 50%. The authors release eight public products and a harness/grader tool. Key limitations include the specialized nature of Replit-based production tasks and the inherent difficulty of scaling long-horizon, state-dependent evaluations in agentic workflows.

papers.title: Suppressing Misaligned Behaviors in Language Models, Durably
papers.abstract: Undesired model behaviors can emerge or re-emerge at any stage of training. Once observed, how effectively can we suppress them? To study this question, we first construct two model organisms--language models deliberately trained to exhibit a specific misalignment--that differ in what triggers the behavior. The narrow-trigger organism misbehaves only when the prompt contains a specific cue: it cheats on multiple-choice questions by following a planted hint that points to a wrong answer, and behaves normally otherwise. The broad-trigger organism has no such cue: after fine-tuning on insecure code, it gives harmful responses across a wide range of open-ended prompts. We then formalize post-hoc behavioral suppression and evaluate methods along three criteria: immediate suppression of the target behavior, durability under further training, and preservation of general capability. We compare standard methods--SFT, GRPO, and gradient-ascent unlearning--along these dimensions. Building on prior work on alignment shallowness, we hypothesize that more durable suppression requires the ability to recover from a wider range of misalignment states. We introduce Prefix-Expanded Adversarial Reinforcement Learning (PEARL), a GRPO variant that augments rollouts with continuations from intermediate states sampled along cached organism trajectories. Across both organism settings and two model families (Qwen3-4B, GPT-OSS-20B), PEARL achieves strong immediate suppression while preserving task accuracy, and remains durable under further fine-tuning on either the organism's data or unrelated data. It obtains the greatest benefit when the undesirable behavior is broad and cannot be addressed through targeted SFT. Together, our framework and method offer a step toward more durable post-hoc removal of undesired behaviors.
papers.what_changed: The authors introduce Prefix-Expanded Adversarial Reinforcement Learning (PEARL), a GRPO-based method that improves the durability of suppressing undesirable model behaviors by training on rollouts from cached intermediate misalignment states.
papers.why_it_matters: Researchers and developers focused on AI safety should care because this method prevents undesirable model behaviors from re-emerging after further fine-tuning, which is a common failure point for current unlearning techniques.

explanations.plain: Imagine you teach a dog a bad habit, like jumping on guests. You might train the dog to stop, but the habit often comes back later when the dog gets excited. In AI, models sometimes 'forget' their safety training when they learn new things, leading old bad behaviors to pop back up. The researchers created a new way to train AI that doesn't just teach it to avoid bad behavior once, but makes that lesson 'stick' even as the AI continues to learn. Think of it like a vaccination that stays effective even if the AI is exposed to new data later. This helps ensure that once a harmful behavior is removed from an AI, it stays gone permanently.
explanations.student: The paper addresses the issue of 'alignment shallowness' in Large Language Models, where post-hoc suppression of undesired behaviors (like bias or harmful code generation) is not durable under further training. The authors define two 'model organisms': a narrow-trigger model (behaving badly only on specific cues) and a broad-trigger model (behaving badly across open-ended prompts). They evaluate standard techniques like Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), and gradient-ascent unlearning. To address the instability of these methods, they propose PEARL (Prefix-Expanded Adversarial Reinforcement Learning). PEARL modifies the GRPO objective by augmenting training rollouts with model continuations sampled from cached trajectories of the misaligned state. This effectively forces the model to learn a more robust representation of the desired state that resists reversion to previous misalignment. Testing on Qwen3-4B and GPT-OSS-20B models, the authors show that PEARL achieves superior durability against subsequent fine-tuning on both related and unrelated datasets. The method is particularly effective for 'broad-trigger' behaviors where targeted SFT fails to generalize. This research formalizes the evaluation of post-hoc unlearning through three lenses: immediate suppression efficacy, durability under fine-tuning, and the preservation of general capabilities.
explanations.expert: The authors investigate the durability of post-hoc behavioral suppression in LLMs, introducing a framework involving two 'model organisms' to represent narrow-trigger (cue-dependent) and broad-trigger (systemic) misalignment. They benchmark SFT, GRPO, and gradient-ascent unlearning, noting that these often fail to prevent re-emergence of prohibited behaviors during subsequent training. Their proposed method, PEARL, is a GRPO variant that samples rollouts from intermediate states stored in a cache of the misaligned model's trajectory. By augmenting the policy gradient objective with these expanded prefixes, PEARL enforces a more robust alignment boundary. Results on Qwen3-4B and GPT-OSS-20B indicate that PEARL provides effective immediate suppression while maintaining task accuracy. Crucially, it demonstrates higher durability under fine-tuning compared to baselines. The improvement is most pronounced for broad-trigger misalignment where standard SFT struggles. Limitations include the computational overhead of caching and the dependency on defining a representative 'organism' for the target behavior. The study contributes to the literature on mechanistic interpretability and unlearning, suggesting that durability is inherently linked to the model's ability to navigate and recover from the latent space of the misaligned trajectory.

papers.title: Hybrid Spark: Adaptive Speculative Decoding That Lets the Content Choose the Drafter
papers.abstract: Speculative decoding (SD) speeds up large language model (LLM) serving, but its gain depends on the workload's \emph{shape}, such as batch size and context length, and on its \emph{content}. A model-based drafter proposes a short block on any content, while a model-free drafter such as n-gram lookup proposes long copies at almost no cost when the output repeats its input, as in code editing. Adaptive verification spends a batch-wide verification budget on the draft tokens most likely to be accepted, but it supports only one model-based drafter. Model-free drafters provide no per-token confidence, so they cannot take part in budget allocation, and deployments must either fix one drafter or split their GPUs between drafters. We present \sys, a framework that runs a model-based and a model-free drafter on every step and gives each request the better of their chains, within adaptive verification and entirely on the GPU, which keeps asynchronous scheduling intact. The key idea is a price per verified draft token: the goodput that slot would earn elsewhere in the batch. Once the model-free drafter's tokens carry calibrated acceptance estimates, fit once on general text, this price puts both drafters' chains on one scale. Instantiated with \dspark and an n-gram drafter in vLLM, \sys achieves 1.10--1.62\x the output throughput of \dspark on code editing at batch size~4 and 1.04--1.27\x at batch size~128, while staying at 0.97--1.01\x of it on chat at temperature~0. A single deployment can therefore serve both workloads.
papers.what_changed: The authors introduce Hybrid Spark, a framework that concurrently runs both model-based and model-free (n-gram) drafters. By using calibrated acceptance estimates for n-grams, it enables adaptive verification to select the optimal draft per request, improving throughput without requiring separate deployments.
papers.why_it_matters: Practitioners can now use a single deployment to serve diverse workloads like code editing and chat efficiently, as the system dynamically chooses the best acceleration strategy for each request.

explanations.plain: Large language models are powerful but slow to generate text. Speculative decoding speeds this up by using a small, fast 'drafter' model to guess the next few words, which a larger model then verifies. Usually, you have to pick one type of guesser. Sometimes, a small model is better; other times, looking for repeating patterns in text is faster. Imagine you are writing an essay and have two assistants: one who knows grammar well and another who is great at copying sentences you already used. If you force one assistant to do both jobs, you lose efficiency. Hybrid Spark allows both assistants to work at once, and the system automatically picks the best suggestion for each sentence, making the whole process significantly faster.
explanations.student: Speculative decoding (SD) accelerates LLM inference by using a fast drafter to propose token sequences, which the target model verifies in parallel. Traditional SD approaches are limited to a single drafter, typically either a small neural network or a non-parametric model like n-gram lookup. While model-based drafters offer general utility, n-gram drafters excel at repetitive tasks like code completion. The core challenge is that existing adaptive verification mechanisms rely on model-based confidence scores, which n-gram drafters lack. Hybrid Spark solves this by calibrating n-gram acceptance probabilities, allowing both drafter types to be evaluated under a unified 'goodput' metric. The system assigns a cost to each draft slot based on the potential throughput gain, effectively integrating both drafters into a single scheduling loop within the vLLM framework. By keeping all computations on the GPU and maintaining asynchronous scheduling, the system optimizes throughput for diverse workloads without splitting GPU resources between separate models.
explanations.expert: Hybrid Spark addresses the limitations of monolithic speculative decoding (SD) by implementing a multi-drafter architecture that concurrently integrates neural and non-parametric n-gram drafters. The framework introduces a unified calibration mechanism that assigns acceptance probability estimates to n-gram tokens, allowing them to compete with neural drafters within an adaptive verification budget. This is achieved by defining a universal cost metric for each verified slot, the expected goodput, which allows the scheduler to dynamically select the highest-utility chain for each request. Experiments within vLLM, using a standard neural drafter (e.g., Eagle/D-Spark), demonstrate throughput improvements of 1.10--1.62x for code editing at batch size 4 and 1.04--1.27x at batch size 128, while maintaining neutral performance (0.97--1.01x) for chat tasks. The primary limitation is the requirement for initial calibration of n-gram acceptance rates on representative text, though once calibrated, it eliminates the need for workload-specific deployment silos or manual model selection. The framework preserves asynchronous scheduling and eliminates the overhead of cross-device data movement by keeping all operations on the GPU.

papers.title: GaussianRenderFormer: Transformer-based Rendering of 3D Gaussian Splats
papers.abstract: Can a neural network learn to render 3D Gaussian splats on its own, with no rasterizer in the renderer? We present GaussianRenderFormer, a transformer that takes a set of Gaussians and a camera and outputs the image directly. Each Gaussian becomes one token in a view-independent encoder, and a view-dependent decoder turns small patches of camera rays into pixels by attending to those tokens. Trained on 26,820 Objaverse objects pruned to 20,000 Gaussians each, GaussianRenderFormer renders 300 unseen objects at 38.08 dB PSNR against the full, unpruned splats, while rasterizing the same pruned input reaches 44.02 dB. The gap is not one of generalization, and our diagnostics are consistent with a bottleneck in the view decoder: telling it the projected footprint of each Gaussian, which it could in principle infer, adds 1.4 dB. Under-training is not ruled out. Code, trained models and videos: https://svlwoof.github.io/gaussianrenderformer
papers.what_changed: The authors introduce GaussianRenderFormer, a transformer-based renderer that generates images from 3D Gaussian Splats without using a traditional explicit rasterizer. The method represents Gaussians as tokens in an encoder and uses a view-dependent decoder to project camera rays into pixels.
papers.why_it_matters: This research challenges the necessity of traditional rasterization pipelines in 3D graphics, offering a path toward fully learned neural rendering systems that could potentially bypass manual projection math.

explanations.plain: Traditional computer graphics rely on a process called rasterization, which is like a strict mathematical rulebook used to paint 3D shapes onto a 2D screen. This paper explores whether an artificial intelligence can learn to paint these shapes from scratch without following those pre-written rules. The researchers built a 'transformer' AI, a type of model often used for understanding language, and trained it to look at a cloud of 3D points and guess how a camera would see them. Think of it like teaching a student to draw a scene by looking at a pile of Lego bricks, rather than giving them a ruler and geometry textbook. While it does not perfectly match the traditional math yet, it shows that neural networks can learn the physics of light and perspective on their own.
explanations.student: GaussianRenderFormer explores an alternative to traditional 3D rasterization by framing rendering as a sequence-to-sequence transformation. In 3D Gaussian Splatting, a scene is represented as a collection of 3D Gaussians. Typically, these are rendered via a specialized hardware-efficient rasterizer that handles alpha-blending and projection. This paper replaces the rasterizer with a transformer architecture. The encoder treats each Gaussian as an individual token, creating a view-independent representation. The decoder then processes camera rays as inputs, attending to the Gaussian tokens to output final pixels. This effectively turns a rendering problem into an attention-based retrieval and projection task. The study utilizes a large-scale training set from the Objaverse dataset, consisting of 26,820 objects. While the model achieves a PSNR of 38.08 dB, it trails the traditional rasterization approach, which hits 44.02 dB on the same input. The authors identify a bottleneck in the view decoder, noting that explicitly providing the projected footprint of Gaussians improves performance, suggesting the model struggles to internally recover geometric projection properties from raw tokenized input alone.
explanations.expert: GaussianRenderFormer investigates replacing the standard differentiable rasterizer in Gaussian Splatting with a transformer-based rendering architecture. The model employs a view-independent encoder where each Gaussian primitive is treated as an input token. A view-dependent decoder then processes small patches of camera rays, utilizing cross-attention to aggregate information from the Gaussian tokens. Experiments were conducted on a subset of the Objaverse dataset, training on 26,820 objects and evaluating on 300 unseen samples. The model achieved a PSNR of 38.08 dB compared to 44.02 dB for traditional rasterization on pruned inputs (20,000 Gaussians per object). Diagnostic experiments revealed that providing the decoder with explicit projected footprint information yields a 1.4 dB increase in PSNR, suggesting that the model encounters a representational bottleneck regarding camera-space projection. The authors conclude that the performance gap is not due to a failure in generalization, but rather limitations in the decoder's ability to infer geometric constraints, alongside potential under-training of the transformer weights. The results indicate that while full neural rendering is viable, implicit geometric reasoning remains a significant challenge compared to explicit rasterization kernels.

papers.title: BrainBind: Bridging Synchronized EEG and fMRI through Long-Form Naturalistic Video Representations
papers.abstract: Real-world vision is dynamic and scene-rich, while EEG and fMRI resolve it at complementary temporal and spatial scales. Most neural decoding systems, however, align one modality in isolation and mostly against static images or short clips. We study the synchronized case: EEG and fMRI are recorded during the same long-form naturalistic viewing, giving a shared stimulus but also recurring narrative context and many semantically similar candidates. We present BrainBind, a framework that maps synchronized EEG and fMRI into frozen long-form video embedding spaces and treats those spaces as common visual-semantic references, not literal neural codes. On CineBrain, a five-seed Recall@K 2 x 4 matrix across two video anchors and four system configurations shows distinct retrieval profiles. With Omni, fMRI organizes the full candidate list most strongly (MRR = 23.82, nDCG@10 = 25.31), while Joint-Dual gives the highest mean label-aware R@1 (13.52%) with a distinct rank-wide profile. The complementary episode-disjoint evaluation quantifies the contribution of repeated stimulus identity and narrative context to the random split. Across these experiments, proxy choice and system configuration produce distinct top-rank and rank-wide retrieval profiles within the present synchronized dataset. The code is available at https://github.com/Forainest789/Brainbind.
papers.what_changed: BrainBind is a framework that maps synchronized EEG and fMRI data into frozen long-form video embedding spaces to serve as a shared visual-semantic reference. It introduces a systematic evaluation on the CineBrain dataset to compare retrieval profiles across different configurations like Omni and Joint-Dual.
papers.why_it_matters: This research provides a new way to align high-resolution brain data with complex, continuous human experiences, which helps scientists better understand how the brain processes long, narrative-based visual inputs.

explanations.plain: Our brains process the world like a continuous movie rather than a series of disconnected snapshots. Scientists use two main tools to observe this: EEG, which tracks the timing of brain signals, and fMRI, which tracks where activity happens. Usually, these are studied separately or with simple images. This paper introduces a system called BrainBind that acts like a translator. It takes these brain signals and tries to match them to specific moments in a long video. Think of it like trying to identify a specific scene in a movie just by looking at a person's heartbeat and blood flow; BrainBind helps computers learn to recognize these patterns so we can better understand how our brains experience complex stories.
explanations.student: BrainBind is a computational framework designed for joint neural decoding, specifically targeting the alignment of electroencephalography (EEG) and functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data. In standard neuroscience tasks, researchers typically decode either temporal resolution from EEG or spatial localization from fMRI using static stimuli. BrainBind instead leverages long-form naturalistic videos, using frozen video embedding spaces as a bridge to align these multimodal signals. By treating these embedding spaces as common visual-semantic references rather than direct neural representations, the authors enable a cross-modal retrieval task. The evaluation uses the CineBrain dataset to test system configurations like 'Omni' and 'Joint-Dual.' The results show that fMRI data provides stronger organization for candidate lists (MRR = 23.82, nDCG@10 = 25.31), while the Joint-Dual configuration excels in label-aware recall metrics. This work highlights how narrative context and repeated stimuli influence the performance of neural decoding models, providing a benchmark for future research in synchronized multimodal brain-computer interfacing.
explanations.expert: BrainBind addresses the challenge of decoding synchronized EEG and fMRI signals by mapping both into frozen, high-dimensional video embedding spaces. Unlike conventional models that process modalities in isolation or against static image datasets, BrainBind treats these embedding spaces as a common manifold to facilitate retrieval tasks within long-form narrative stimuli. The authors present the CineBrain dataset and evaluate four system configurations. The Omni configuration demonstrates high structural alignment for fMRI, achieving an MRR of 23.82 and nDCG@10 of 25.31. Conversely, the Joint-Dual configuration yields superior label-aware recall, with an R@1 of 13.52%. The methodology includes an episode-disjoint evaluation to disentangle the effects of stimulus identity from narrative context, clarifying how different proxy choices affect retrieval profiles. A key constraint is the dependence on the frozen video encoder, which limits the latent semantic capacity to the quality of the pre-trained model. This study provides a rigorous framework for benchmarking multimodal decoding architectures in naturalistic conditions, with the full codebase accessible via the authors' GitHub repository.

papers.title: Recursive Sparse Attention: Million-Token Length Extrapolation at Logarithmic Cost
papers.abstract: At context lengths of about 1M tokens, dense attention is costly in prefill and decoding, and training typically relies on long documents, which become scarcer as the target length increases. Most sparse attention methods score all preceding blocks or tokens, so their selection cost per query is $O(L)$ at context length $L$; hierarchical selection reduces it to $O(\log L)$, but prior trainable hierarchical methods report accuracy only within their training length. We propose RecSA (Recursive Sparse Attention), which builds a tree over the KV cache in which each node summarizes its subtree with one key and one mean-pooled value. The keys come from one pooler per layer, shared by all levels and distilled from dense attention. Each level above the tokens selects at most $k$ candidates, so each query has $O(\log L)$ selection cost and reads $O(\log L)$ entries; the summaries of unselected candidates share one softmax with the exact tokens. Each entry's RoPE position is its index among the candidates of its level, so at any length every relative distance stays within the range seen during training. Initialized from Qwen3-4B and trained on 0.62B tokens at the original model's 32K training length, RecSA outperforms all baselines on RULER at every length from 131K to 2M; at 1M, it scores 60.5, compared with 40.0 for the best baseline, Dense + DCA. With our optimized kernels, RecSA is faster than dense attention in end-to-end prefill and decoding from 64K to 2M; at 524K on one H200 GPU, it accelerates prefill by 3.2x and decoding by 3.8x.
papers.what_changed: The authors introduce RecSA (Recursive Sparse Attention), a method that organizes the KV cache into a tree structure to achieve logarithmic selection cost. By using a shared pooler to summarize subtrees, it enables context extrapolation up to 2 million tokens while maintaining relative position stability.
papers.why_it_matters: Researchers and practitioners dealing with massive context windows will benefit from the reduced computational overhead and improved accuracy on long-range tasks like RULER, which previously suffered from performance degradation at extreme lengths.

explanations.plain: Modern AI models struggle to process million-word books because they try to keep track of every single word at once, which becomes slow and expensive. Imagine you are asked to summarize a library, but you can only look at one shelf at a time. Instead of looking at every book individually, you might look at a sign on each shelf that tells you what kind of books are there. RecSA acts like this sign system for AI. It organizes information into a tree, allowing the model to quickly narrow down the most important parts without reading every single word in detail. This allows the AI to handle massive amounts of text much faster and more accurately than previous methods.
explanations.student: Recursive Sparse Attention (RecSA) addresses the O(L) bottleneck of traditional attention mechanisms in long-context language models. In dense attention, every query attends to every key-value (KV) pair, making computation grow linearly with context length. RecSA constructs a tree over the KV cache where each node represents a summarized subtree using one key and a mean-pooled value. This hierarchical structure reduces the selection cost per query to O(log L). The keys are generated via a layer-shared pooler distilled from dense attention. A key feature is the handling of positional embeddings; by using the index within the candidate level as the RoPE (Rotary Positional Embedding) position, the model ensures that relative distances remain within the range observed during training, which is critical for length extrapolation. Experiments starting from a 32K context Qwen3-4B base demonstrate that RecSA achieves strong performance at 2 million tokens, significantly outperforming dense attention and common sparse baselines on the RULER benchmark. Additionally, custom kernels provide up to 3.8x speedups in decoding at 524K tokens, demonstrating high hardware efficiency.
explanations.expert: RecSA optimizes long-context attention by moving from O(L) to O(log L) query-key selection via a recursive tree structure over the KV cache. Each node summarizes its subtree as (key, mean_pooled_value), with keys derived from a layer-shared pooler distilled from dense attention. A primary technical innovation is the RoPE implementation: each entry's position is relative to its index among candidates at that specific level, effectively keeping relative distances within the 32K training window regardless of total sequence length. The model, initialized from Qwen3-4B, was trained on 0.62B tokens and evaluated on RULER. It achieves a score of 60.5 at 1M tokens vs 40.0 for Dense + DCA. In throughput tests on a single H200, RecSA yields 3.2x prefill and 3.8x decoding speedups at 524K tokens. Limitations primarily involve the reliance on distilled poolers and the overhead of maintaining the recursive tree structure, though optimized kernels demonstrate significant practical gains across the 64K to 2M token range.

papers.title: Multi-step SWE: Can Coding Agents Keep Building on Their Own Code Over Long Horizons?
papers.abstract: Developers rarely give a coding agent a single request: they ask it to build a component and then to extend, upgrade, and optimize it, each time on code the agent itself wrote. Most benchmarks, however, score one task at a time. We introduce Multi-step SWE, a long-horizon benchmark of 69 software engineering tasks, each a chain of 5-15 dependent steps on a single codebase. Every step is a complete, multi-hour engineering request that starts from the code the agent produced in the preceding steps, so early design decisions and errors carry forward. The tasks span four families of engineering work and nine languages, include both from-scratch builds and existing open-source codebases, and ground every step in an existing source of truth that defines both the instruction and its verifier. Across nine frontier models, the strongest model reaches a solve rate of only 18.5%, and 38 of the 69 tasks are not solved by any model. We release Multi-step SWE publicly at https://multistepswe.com.
papers.what_changed: The authors introduce Multi-step SWE, a benchmark consisting of 69 long-horizon software engineering tasks where each task requires 5-15 dependent steps built sequentially upon the agent's previous code.
papers.why_it_matters: It challenges current coding agents by testing their ability to maintain consistency and handle accumulated technical debt over extended development sessions, which reflects real-world programming workflows better than single-turn evaluations.

explanations.plain: Most AI coding tools are tested by asking them to solve one task at a time, like writing a single function or fixing one bug. However, real software development is a continuous process where you build a feature, then upgrade it, and later optimize it based on what you wrote earlier. If an AI makes a bad design choice in the first step, it might struggle to fix it later. This paper introduces a new testing system called Multi-step SWE. It forces AI models to work through a chain of 5 to 15 related tasks. It is like asking a chef to cook a meal over several hours rather than just asking for a single pre-made dish. The results show that even advanced models struggle when they have to live with their own past mistakes.
explanations.student: Current evaluations for Software Engineering (SE) agents predominantly focus on single-turn tasks. Multi-step SWE introduces a long-horizon benchmark consisting of 69 tasks, where each task involves a sequence of 5-15 interdependent engineering requests. The core challenge here is state persistence and the accumulation of technical debt: because each step requires the agent to work on code it generated in the previous iteration, errors in early design decisions propagate throughout the entire development lifecycle. The benchmark covers four categories of software engineering tasks across nine programming languages, utilizing existing open-source codebases to provide a ground-truth verifier for each step. The authors evaluated nine frontier models, finding that the highest performing model achieved a solve rate of only 18.5%, with 38 out of 69 tasks remaining completely unsolved by any model tested. This highlights a significant gap in the capabilities of current Large Language Models (LLMs) when transitioning from isolated coding tasks to sustained, multi-step development processes.
explanations.expert: Multi-step SWE addresses the limitation of current SE benchmarks that treat coding as a stateless, single-turn operation. The framework proposes a chain-based evaluation methodology where an agent's output from step $n$ serves as the input repository state for step $n+1$. The dataset comprises 69 sequences, each requiring 5-15 dependent steps, spanning 9 languages and diverse engineering workflows. The primary contribution is the grounding of every step in a verifiable ground-truth, allowing for the quantification of error propagation and long-horizon planning performance. Empirical evaluation across nine state-of-the-art models reveals a substantial performance ceiling: the best-performing model reaches a solve rate of only 18.5%, and over half of the tasks (38/69) are not solved by any model. These results suggest that current autoregressive coding agents lack the robustness required for iterative development, specifically regarding their inability to recover from cascading errors in multi-step trajectories. The benchmark is available at https://multistepswe.com.

papers.title: Measuring AI Agents as Teammates with Collaborative Intelligence
papers.abstract: Progress in AI is often measured by what a single model can do on its own. Yet teams of AI agents are starting to make breakthroughs and discoveries in science, medicine, mathematics and software engineering. As AI begins to work in teams of agents and people, the ability to collaborate becomes a core part of their intelligence. Research on human teams has measured this ability for decades. Inspired by this, we introduce the Collaborative Intelligence Benchmark, which measures how well an AI agent works as a teammate. It contains 240 tasks across 8 dimensions of teamwork, from refusing an unsafe shortcut to checking the work that a weaker model leaves behind. Each task comes from a real record or an existing benchmark, from aviation accident reports and clinical cases to coding tasks and negotiations, and has a programmatically verifiable outcome. To isolate teamwork from individual capability, models are scored only on tasks that they can solve by themselves when they have full information. We evaluate 18 closed- and open-weight models and find that every model, across sizes and families, has clear weaknesses as a teammate, with the best model scoring only 82.2 out of 100. Frontier models almost always refuse unsafe shortcuts and report misconduct, yet they cave under interpersonal pressure, reaching the best overall deal in only 14% of conflicts, and their pass rate drops from 97% to 81% when they take over a task in which a weaker model has cheated. Crucially, general capability does not guarantee good teamwork, as models with nearly the same capability score differ by up to 11 points as teammates. The benchmark includes 160 public tasks with code and data, along with 80 held-out tasks for evaluation. As AI agents increasingly work alongside other agents and people, the ability to collaborate effectively is becoming a crucial capability to measure and develop.
papers.what_changed: The authors introduce the Collaborative Intelligence Benchmark, which evaluates AI agents on 240 tasks across 8 dimensions of teamwork. It specifically isolates collaborative performance from individual competency by ensuring models are only scored on tasks they are already capable of solving solo.
papers.why_it_matters: As AI models transition from solitary tools to collaborative teammates, this benchmark provides a standardized way to measure their ability to work effectively with humans and other AI, revealing that high capability does not equate to effective collaboration.

explanations.plain: We usually judge AI by what it can do alone, like answering a question or writing code. But in the real world, the best work happens in teams. Imagine a brilliant employee who is incredibly smart but refuses to share information, ignores warnings from coworkers, or panics when forced to correct someone else's mistake. That person would be a bad teammate. This research introduces a new test called the Collaborative Intelligence Benchmark. It puts AI models in scenarios where they must work with others, such as checking a colleague's work, navigating a conflict, or refusing an unsafe shortcut. The results show that even the smartest AI models today struggle to be good teammates, suggesting that being clever is not the same as being a good collaborator.
explanations.student: The Collaborative Intelligence Benchmark (CIB) is a new suite of 240 tasks designed to evaluate the multi-agent and human-AI collaborative capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs). A central challenge in measuring 'teamwork' is the confounding variable of individual capability; a model might fail a collaborative task simply because it lacks the underlying knowledge to solve it. To address this, the authors filter the benchmark so that agents are only tested on tasks they demonstrate mastery over individually. The evaluation covers 8 dimensions, including ethics, communication, and error correction. By testing 18 different closed- and open-weight models, the researchers demonstrate a significant 'collaboration gap.' For instance, while frontier models perform well on safety alignment, they struggle significantly in negotiation scenarios, succeeding in only 14% of conflicts. Furthermore, the performance drop observed when agents take over tasks from 'weaker' models suggests that current architectures are not well-optimized for the nuanced inter-agent dynamics required in cooperative environments. This research highlights that as we move toward agentic workflows, benchmarking must shift from individual reasoning to social and collaborative competency.
explanations.expert: This paper presents the Collaborative Intelligence Benchmark (CIB), a comprehensive framework comprising 240 tasks across 8 dimensions of team-oriented AI behavior. The methodology addresses a critical bottleneck in multi-agent evaluation: disentangling collaborative proficiency from individual task competency. By restricting the evaluation to tasks within the agent's baseline capability, confirmed through individual-solve filtering, the authors isolate collaborative heuristics. The benchmark includes diverse domains such as aviation accident analysis and clinical diagnostics. Testing 18 state-of-the-art models, the authors report a performance ceiling of 82.2/100, indicating that current scaling does not automatically confer collaborative intelligence. Notable results include a 16% drop in success rates when inheriting tasks from underperforming agents and a 14% success rate in conflict-heavy negotiations. The study identifies a delta of up to 11 points in collaboration scores between models with similar general capabilities, confirming that collaborative behavior is an independent trait requiring specific optimization. The release includes 160 public tasks with programmatically verifiable outcomes, providing a standardized environment for future research into agentic alignment and coordination protocols.

papers.title: Dory1.0-4B: A Looped Normalized-GPT
papers.abstract: We introduce Dory1.0-4B, a 4-billion-parameter looped (latent-recurrent) language model with elastic depth: a single checkpoint serves different inference compute budgets. Dory1.0-4B is built on a normalized Transformer (nGPT) backbone with interleaved sliding-window and full-attention layers, organized into an input block, a shared recurrent block, and an output block. At inference, the recurrent block can be applied a variable number of times. We pre-trained Dory1.0-4B on 6 trillion tokens. The first 4.5 trillion tokens were trained in NVFP4, and additional pre-training then extended the context length to 256K tokens. Next, we post-trained the model using Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR), with a difficulty-aware loop curriculum that routes harder prompts to deeper loops. Increasing the loop count improves accuracy, with the largest gains on coding, agentic, and long-context benchmarks. With two or more loops, Dory1.0-4B outperforms larger models such as Qwen3.5-9B, Gemma 4 12B, and Gemma 4 26B-A4B on average across 12 benchmarks. Looping also makes Dory1.0-4B more token-efficient on agentic benchmarks: with four loops, it generates 1.3-2.5x fewer tokens than with one loop, as the extra computation is spent in latent space rather than on longer outputs. To reduce memory during looping, Dory1.0-4B caches keys and values only from the last loop, keeping its KV-cache footprint equal to that of a non-looped model at any loop count while retaining most of the accuracy gains. We open-source the BF16, MXFP8, NVFP4, and GGUF quantized checkpoints.
papers.what_changed: Dory1.0-4B introduces a looped, latent-recurrent architecture based on normalized Transformer (nGPT) blocks that allows a single 4B-parameter checkpoint to utilize variable inference compute budgets through a shared recurrent block. papers.why_it_matters: Researchers and practitioners looking to balance inference compute with model performance will benefit from this elastic depth approach. It offers a way to scale performance on complex tasks like coding and agentic workflows without needing separate models for different compute constraints.

explanations.plain: Imagine you are trying to solve a complex math problem. Sometimes a quick glance is enough, but for harder problems, you need to sit and think about it for a while. Dory1.0-4B works exactly like this. Most AI models are 'fixed depth,' meaning they use the same amount of effort regardless of whether the question is easy or hard. Dory, however, uses a 'looped' design. For simple prompts, it processes information quickly. For difficult tasks like coding or logical reasoning, it cycles through a 'thinking' block multiple times. This allows one single AI model to adjust its brainpower based on the problem at hand, saving energy and time while still being smart enough to outperform much larger, static models.

Unlike standard Transformers where layers are executed sequentially once, Dory consists of an input block, a shared recurrent block, and an output block. The recurrent block allows for iterative processing of latent representations. During training, the model used a curriculum that routes harder prompts to more loop iterations. This approach yields significant efficiency gains, particularly in agentic benchmarks, by increasing compute in the latent space rather than relying on chain-of-thought token generation. The model maintains a constant memory footprint for its KV-cache by only caching keys and values from the final loop iteration. It is based on the normalized Transformer (nGPT) architecture and was trained on 6 trillion tokens, including an extension to 256K context length. The model topology separates layers into input, shared recurrent, and output blocks. The 'elastic depth' mechanism allows adjusting inference compute via loop count, specifically trained via a difficulty-aware curriculum incorporating SFT and RLVR. By iterating the recurrent block, the model achieves better performance on coding and agentic tasks compared to larger baselines like Qwen3.5-9B and Gemma 4 series (12B and 26B-A4B). papers.title: SLATE: A Large-Scale Benchmark for Long-Horizon API Selection in E-commerce Tool Use
papers.abstract: Enterprises increasingly want LLM agents to automate standard operating procedures over their software stacks -- mapping each step of a procedure to the right call among thousands of internal APIs, without hand-authored step-to-API mappings. The core difficulty is API selection at scale: choosing and composing the correct tools over a long horizon, judged only by whether the overall task succeeds. Current tool-use benchmarks do not test this regime -- they expose only a handful of tools, evaluate single-step invocation, or grade multi-step behavior with subjective LLM-as-a-judge scores that penalize valid alternative trajectories.
