We introduce SLATE (Synthetic Large-scale API Toolkit for E-commerce), a large-scale benchmark that tests large-toolset, long-horizon API selection in a realistic enterprise domain. SLATE couples (i) queries decomposed into hierarchical, tool-grounded procedures over a ~1,000-tool e-commerce library, (ii) a deterministic, context-aware simulator that returns recorded outputs for matching calls and default responses otherwise, and (iii) an end-to-end task-success metric -- a task succeeds when it reaches every reference outcome -- that credits diverse-but-valid trajectories while remaining fully automatic and reproducible. Experiments with six open decision models and the language models they are built on, from 3B to 12B parameters, show that even the best model completes only 5.0% of the tasks, establishing SLATE as a challenging testbed for reliable enterprise tool use. We release SLATE, its simulator, and the evaluation harness at https://geshijoker.github.io/slate/
papers.what_changed: SLATE is a new large-scale benchmark containing approximately 1,000 APIs in an e-commerce domain designed to evaluate long-horizon tool selection, utilizing a deterministic simulator and an objective, end-to-end task-success metric.
papers.why_it_matters: It addresses the limitation of current benchmarks that only test small toolsets or rely on subjective grading, providing a realistic, reproducible environment for testing how well AI agents can execute complex, multi-step enterprise workflows.

explanations.plain: Imagine you are trying to bake a complex wedding cake, but you have a thousand different kitchen gadgets and you are not sure which one does what. You have to pick the right tool for every single step, like mixing, heating, or frosting, and if you mess up one step, the whole cake fails. Currently, AI research struggles with this because most tests only give the AI a few tools to work with or grade it using another AI that might be biased. SLATE is like a massive, realistic test kitchen for AI. It gives the AI a huge library of a thousand tools and only cares about whether the final result is perfect. It is a much harder, more realistic test for helpful digital assistants.
explanations.student: SLATE (Synthetic Large-scale API Toolkit for E-commerce) is a benchmark designed for evaluating LLM agents in tool-use scenarios where the agent must perform long-horizon, multi-step API calls. Current tool-use benchmarks typically suffer from 'evaluation bias' where they rely on LLM-as-a-judge scores or limit the search space to a small number of tools. SLATE tackles this by providing a library of ~1,000 APIs, mimicking a real-world enterprise software stack. The benchmark uses a deterministic, context-aware simulator that records API outputs, allowing for automated, reproducible testing. The core evaluation metric is an end-to-end task-success criterion, which verifies if the agent achieves the required reference outcomes across a sequence of calls. This moves away from subjective scoring, instead rewarding the agent for reaching the correct goal regardless of the specific valid trajectory taken. By testing models ranging from 3B to 12B parameters, the authors reveal that current state-of-the-art agents achieve only a 5.0% success rate, highlighting the difficulty of long-horizon planning and large-scale API selection in automated workflows.
explanations.expert: SLATE introduces a challenging benchmark for long-horizon API selection, specifically targeting enterprise-scale tool-use environments with ~1,000 internal APIs. The benchmark addresses shortcomings in existing datasets that utilize restricted action spaces or rely on subjective LLM-based evaluation metrics. The SLATE framework comprises a hierarchical procedure decomposition, a deterministic, context-aware simulator that validates output consistency, and an objective end-to-end success metric. By measuring task completion based on reaching predefined reference outcomes, the benchmark accommodates diverse execution trajectories while maintaining reproducibility. The authors evaluate six open-source decision models (3B-12B parameters), demonstrating that even top-performing models struggle with the complexity of the domain, achieving only a 5.0% success rate. This indicates that current agentic workflows fail when scaling to large toolsets and multi-step reasoning tasks. The simulator and evaluation harness are released to facilitate future research in reliable, multi-step API orchestration. Limitations are implicit in the synthetic nature of the e-commerce domain and the performance bottleneck observed in current LLM-based agents, suggesting a significant gap in long-horizon reasoning and planning capabilities.

papers.title: Variational Functional Neural Networks (vfNN)
papers.abstract: We present a variational functional neural network (vfNN) algorithm that optimizes physically motivated continuum functionals in integral form (e.g., Lagrangian, Hamiltonian, or free energy) to find the states of a system. That way, vfNN bypasses solving the equations of motion (a.k.a. the Euler-Lagrange equations), which are in the form of differential equations. To this end, our approach is fundamentally different from conventional physics-informed neural networks (PINN) that solve differential equations by minimizing a phenomenological loss function involving higher order derivatives and ad hoc weight factors. In contrast, vfNN merely evaluates lower order derivatives of the generating functional and replaces the weight factors with rigorous physical scales. This also fundamentally changes the loss landscape, and the desired solutions may become unstable. For this emergent nonconvex optimization problem, we develop a quasi-Newton optimization algorithm with simulated annealing that converges to the solutions of the corresponding Euler-Lagrange equations of the functional regardless of their stability properties. Our simulations using vfNN give accurate results for benchmark systems governed by linear or nonlinear ordinary differential equations.
papers.what_changed: The authors introduce Variational Functional Neural Networks (vfNN), a method that solves physics problems by optimizing integral-based continuum functionals rather than solving differential equations directly.
papers.why_it_matters: It offers an alternative to traditional physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) by avoiding the complexity of higher-order derivative loss functions and ad-hoc weighting parameters.

explanations.plain: Imagine you are trying to find the shortest path between two points on a bumpy landscape. Usually, scientists do this by solving complex math equations that describe the slope at every single point. This is like trying to find your way by calculating the exact tilt of the ground beneath your feet constantly. The new vfNN method works differently. Instead of looking at the local slope, it looks at the total 'energy' of the entire journey. By minimizing this total energy directly, it finds the path without needing to solve those difficult individual slope equations. It is like looking at a map of the whole area to pick the best path at once, which can be much simpler and more robust.
explanations.student: Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) typically encode physical laws into neural networks by minimizing a loss function based on differential equations. This often requires calculating higher-order derivatives and tuning ad-hoc weight factors to balance different parts of the loss. The Variational Functional Neural Network (vfNN) shifts this paradigm. Instead of solving the Euler-Lagrange differential equations, vfNN optimizes the integral-based continuum functionals (such as Lagrangian or free energy) directly. This method uses lower-order derivatives, which simplifies the computational overhead. Because this approach transforms the problem into a challenging, non-convex optimization landscape where solutions might become unstable, the authors introduce a quasi-Newton optimization algorithm integrated with simulated annealing. This combination ensures convergence to the correct solutions even when traditional methods struggle with stability. By focusing on the functional integral rather than the differential equation form, vfNN provides a new way to solve complex systems governed by both linear and nonlinear ordinary differential equations.
explanations.expert: The authors propose Variational Functional Neural Networks (vfNN) as an alternative to traditional PINNs for solving systems governed by continuum functionals. While PINNs generally minimize residuals of Euler-Lagrange (EL) equations, requiring high-order derivatives and manual hyperparameter tuning for loss balancing, vfNN optimizes the integral-based functional itself. This results in a loss landscape characterized by lower-order derivatives and rigorous physical scaling, replacing arbitrary weighting. To address the resulting non-convex optimization, the authors implement a quasi-Newton optimizer augmented with simulated annealing. This framework converges to the ground-truth solutions of EL equations regardless of their stability properties. The authors validate the method on linear and nonlinear ordinary differential equation (ODE) benchmarks, demonstrating high accuracy. A key technical advantage is the avoidance of higher-order derivative computation, which often introduces numerical instability and significant computational cost in deep learning-based physics solvers. By operating directly on the variational functional, vfNN mitigates the need for phenomenological loss definitions, providing a more theoretically grounded approach to solving physical systems.

papers.title: ProteoCraft: Protein Design as Proposal-Verification Search
papers.abstract: Protein-protein interactions underpin nearly all biological processes. Yet, designing proteins with desired interactions remains challenging due to the structural complexity governing molecular recognition. This study views protein design as a search optimization problem over a combinatorial sequence space under expensive structural evaluation. Toward this goal, we introduce a novel tree-based search framework, ProteoCraft, that employs approximate structural gradients from diffusion-based structure predictors as effective proposal policies to specify where the search should explore. Complete no-gradient inference of folding models separately assigns values to the resulting sequences, determining what is good. ProteoCraft allocates this verification budget through a coarse-to-fine paradigm: multi-site edits first explore distinct sequence basins, then verified promising states undergo strict single-site refinement. Across fourteen de novo binder-design settings spanning eight target proteins, five immune-relevant TCR-facing targets, and four localized CDR redesign tasks, ProteoCraft improves design quality and high-confidence yield. These improvements persist under independent AF2-IG and Rosetta-based interface evaluation. Prospective experimental validation further yielded an 82.9% binding hit rate for PD-L1 miniproteins, with a best measured KD of 0.879 nM, and confirmed binding of designed IFNAR2 VHH. Our code is available at https://github.com/smiles724/ProteoCraft_v1.
papers.what_changed: ProteoCraft is a new tree-based search framework for protein design that uses approximate structural gradients from diffusion-based models to guide sequence exploration and a coarse-to-fine verification process to validate candidates.
papers.why_it_matters: It offers a more efficient way to design proteins for specific biological interactions, demonstrated by high success rates in laboratory experiments for complex targets like PD-L1.

explanations.plain: Designing a new protein is like searching for a specific key in a giant, invisible library. You need to build a structure that fits perfectly into a target lock, like a virus or a cell receptor. ProteoCraft acts like a smart librarian who uses a two-step process: first, it makes broad guesses about where to look based on general patterns (coarse search), and then it focuses deeply on the most promising leads to verify if they work (fine refinement). This system significantly speeds up the design process compared to trial-and-error. When tested in the real world, it successfully created molecules that bind to their targets with high precision, performing much better than previous computational methods.
explanations.student: ProteoCraft frames de novo protein design as a combinatorial search optimization problem. The core challenge is exploring a massive sequence space where evaluating the structural fitness of a candidate is computationally expensive. ProteoCraft employs a tree-based search framework where the exploration policy is guided by approximate structural gradients derived from pre-trained diffusion-based structure predictors. These predictors act as a proposal mechanism. The framework then utilizes a coarse-to-fine verification strategy: it initially explores broad sequence basins via multi-site edits before shifting to single-site refinements for high-value states. Value assessment is decoupled from the proposal mechanism by using gradient-free folding model inference. This approach addresses the problem of 'black-box' structural evaluation. By effectively managing the computational budget for verification, the method improves design quality and yield across diverse benchmarks, including binder design and CDR (Complementarity-Determining Region) redesign. It demonstrates robustness against external evaluation tools like AF2-IG and Rosetta. The authors report an 82.9% binding hit rate for PD-L1 miniproteins and successful prospective experimental validation for IFNAR2 VHH, showing strong alignment between computational predictions and physical binding affinity.
explanations.expert: ProteoCraft is a tree-based search framework designed to optimize protein sequences under expensive structural evaluation. It addresses the combinatorial explosion of sequence space by partitioning the problem into proposal and verification phases. The proposal policy leverages approximate structural gradients from diffusion-based structure predictors to bias the search toward favorable sequence regions. Verification is performed using gradient-free folding inference in a coarse-to-fine paradigm: multi-site edits facilitate basin exploration, while single-site refinements solidify promising states. Evaluated across 14 de novo binder-design settings, the method consistently outperforms baselines, maintaining improved design quality under independent AF2-IG and Rosetta interface evaluations. Empirical results are strong, yielding an 82.9% hit rate for PD-L1 miniproteins with a best KD of 0.879 nM, and successful binding confirmation for IFNAR2 VHH. The decoupled nature of the proposal and verification steps effectively mitigates the gradient requirements of the folding model, though reliance on existing folding models for evaluation remains a structural dependency.

papers.title: Library of Layers (LoL): Adaptively Ordering Transformer Layers at Runtime
papers.abstract: Computer programmers chain together the same reusable computational primitives, for example, conditional statements or loops, but in different orders to implement different algorithms. In contrast, existing language model architectures always execute their layers in the same order. We introduce Library of Layers (LoL), an architecture that dynamically orders its layers during inference to solve the problem at hand. LoL has a single hyperparameter, the size of its global library of transformer blocks, that allows it to transition seamlessly between parameter reuse and sparsity, generalizing the parameter-efficiency and FLOPs-efficiency tradeoffs of dense, depth-recurrent, and mixture of experts architectures in one unified family. We show that LoL achieves competitive performance with all three above baselines when pretrained on text data. On synthetic sudoku and maze data, we observe that the model employs distinct layer orderings to implement different solution strategies, and we can intervene on routing to force a model to apply a specific solution strategy to a problem instance. In a multilingual natural language setting, we find that LoL chooses different layer order patterns based on language and script. Similarly, we train LoL on safety data and fit probes to its router outputs, finding that these probes distinguish safe from unsafe text with high AUROC. LoL provides a path toward a future in which models dynamically compose their own computational graph, enabling more efficient and controllable reasoning.
papers.what_changed: The authors introduce Library of Layers (LoL), an architecture that dynamically reorders transformer layers during inference rather than executing them in a fixed, predefined sequence.
papers.why_it_matters: LoL enables models to adaptively select computational paths based on specific inputs, offering potential improvements in parameter efficiency, controllability, and reasoning capabilities.

explanations.plain: Imagine you are following a recipe to cook a meal. Currently, most AI models follow a strict, unchangeable list of steps every single time, regardless of whether they are making a sandwich or a gourmet dinner. The Library of Layers (LoL) changes this by giving the AI a toolbox of different cooking techniques. When the AI is given a task, it decides in real-time which order to use these techniques to solve the problem most efficiently. It is like having a chef who can reorder the steps of a recipe on the fly based on what ingredients are available. By choosing the right sequence for each specific request, the model becomes more flexible, better at complex reasoning, and more efficient with its computational power.
explanations.student: In standard transformer architectures, layers are organized in a static, feed-forward stack. The Library of Layers (LoL) breaks this paradigm by introducing dynamic routing at inference time. The architecture consists of a library of transformer blocks where the model learns to sequence these blocks adaptively. This approach effectively unifies the operational paradigms of dense, depth-recurrent, and mixture of experts (MoE) models under a single framework defined by a hyperparameter controlling the library size. From an algorithmic perspective, LoL treats computation as an ordered sequence of function calls. By training on synthetic tasks like Sudoku, the authors demonstrate that the model learns distinct 'strategies' represented by specific layer orderings. This routing behavior is not merely opaque; the researchers show that routing patterns correlate with language, script, and content safety. Specifically, by training probes on the router's output, they achieved high AUROC in identifying unsafe text. This suggests that LoL provides a more interpretable and controllable reasoning structure. For students of deep learning, this is a transition from static computation graphs to dynamic, input-conditioned graph construction, which has significant implications for both inference-time efficiency and the modularity of large-scale models.
explanations.expert: Library of Layers (LoL) is a novel architectural framework that moves away from fixed-depth transformer sequences, instead allowing for dynamic, input-dependent layer ordering at runtime. LoL generalizes across parameter-efficient and FLOP-efficient architectures, effectively subsuming dense, depth-recurrent, and MoE models depending on the hyperparameter setting of the library size. The architecture functions by dynamically scheduling transformer block execution, allowing the model to implement different strategies per task instance. Empirical results on synthetic domains, such as Sudoku and maze navigation, reveal that the model learns specific, identifiable routing policies. When intervened upon, the model confirms these policies are causal to the solution path. In multilingual settings, LoL exhibits distinct routing patterns conditioned on the input language and script. Furthermore, safety probes applied to the router's decisions demonstrate that the learned routing logic carries high-level semantic information, achieving high AUROC in safety classification tasks. The primary contribution is the demonstration that adaptive graph composition is feasible and useful for controllability. Limitations are implicitly suggested by the reliance on runtime routing overhead, which requires further investigation into hardware-level integration for latency gains compared to traditional static-graph optimizations.

papers.title: Architecture-Aware Mixed Precision for Replica-Exchange Training of Geometry-Aware Neural Operators with Uncertainty Quantification
papers.abstract: Geometry-aware neural operators face substantial computational and memory demands when learning across complex physical domains. We introduce Architecture-Aware Mixed Precision (AA-MP), a replica-exchange training strategy that allocates numerical precision according to replica roles and architecture-specific operations. By retaining FP32 for refinement while selectively employing BF16 for exploration, AA-MP preserves predictive accuracy while improving training efficiency. Across fluid dynamics and three-dimensional structural mechanics benchmarks, AA-MP achieves comparable accuracy to full-precision training over an ensemble of runs, while reducing hot-replica peak GPU memory by 46.9% and training time by up to 25.8%. It also outperforms naive Automatic Mixed Precision (AMP) in memory efficiency and computational cost, with increasing memory advantages at larger model and geometry scales. Ablation studies show that retaining FP32 in the cold-replica is important for predictive accuracy, while additional FP32 operations in the exploratory replica provide limited benefits relative to their computational cost. Finally, conformal prediction for uncertainty calibration shows that AA-MP achieves near-nominal coverage with narrower prediction intervals than the alternatives. These results advance the scalability of geometry-aware scientific machine learning by reducing computational costs without compromising predictive accuracy or uncertainty quantification.
papers.what_changed: The authors introduce Architecture-Aware Mixed Precision (AA-MP), a training strategy for geometry-aware neural operators that assigns different numerical precisions (FP32 vs BF16) based on replica roles within a replica-exchange framework.
papers.why_it_matters: Researchers and engineers working on large-scale scientific simulations can use this to significantly reduce memory consumption and training time without sacrificing model accuracy or the quality of uncertainty estimates.

explanations.plain: Training AI models to simulate complex physical systems like fluid flow or structural stress is very expensive, often requiring massive amounts of computer memory and time. These models work by creating multiple variations of themselves, called replicas, to explore different solutions. The researchers developed a method called Architecture-Aware Mixed Precision (AA-MP) that manages how much detail, or precision, each replica uses. Imagine a team of architects building a complex bridge; some team members need to do precise measurements to finalize the design, while others just need a rough sketch to explore ideas. By letting the 'explorers' use less-detailed math and keeping the 'refiners' at high detail, the system becomes faster and leaner. This approach cuts memory usage by nearly half and speeds up training significantly.
explanations.student: Geometry-aware neural operators are models designed to learn mappings between infinite-dimensional function spaces, which are essential for solving partial differential equations. However, these models are computationally intensive. The authors propose Architecture-Aware Mixed Precision (AA-MP), a strategy integrated into a replica-exchange training framework. Replica exchange involves running multiple model instances (replicas) that interact to explore the solution space more effectively. AA-MP optimizes this by dynamically assigning numerical precision, using full 32-bit floating point (FP32) for refinement replicas and 16-bit Brain Floating Point (BF16) for exploration replicas. This selective precision assignment acknowledges that different parts of the architecture have varying sensitivities to rounding errors. By strategically using lower precision where it is computationally expensive but mathematically less critical, the authors achieve a 46.9% reduction in peak GPU memory and a 25.8% reduction in training time compared to standard training. Furthermore, they incorporate conformal prediction, a statistical framework for quantifying uncertainty, to ensure the model provides valid prediction intervals. This demonstrates that efficiency gains do not necessitate a trade-off in predictive reliability or the robustness of uncertainty estimates in high-dimensional scientific domains.
explanations.expert: This paper presents Architecture-Aware Mixed Precision (AA-MP), a specialized training regime for geometry-aware neural operators. The method leverages replica-exchange training, applying BF16 to exploratory replicas and FP32 to refinement replicas. This selective precision strategy mitigates the memory overhead associated with high-resolution physical simulations. Benchmarked on fluid dynamics and 3D structural mechanics, AA-MP achieves a 46.9% reduction in peak GPU memory usage and up to 25.8% speedup over full-precision training. The authors compare AA-MP against naive Automatic Mixed Precision (AMP), reporting superior scaling in memory efficiency as model complexity increases. Ablation studies confirm that maintaining FP32 in cold-replicas is critical for predictive accuracy, whereas excessive FP32 usage in exploratory replicas yields diminishing returns. Notably, the framework integrates conformal prediction for uncertainty quantification, achieving near-nominal coverage with tighter intervals than baseline methods. Limitations are primarily context-dependent; the strategy assumes a replica-exchange setup and is tuned for neural operators where precision requirements vary by architectural component rather than just tensor data types. The results suggest a viable pathway for scaling scientific machine learning tasks on resource-constrained hardware without compromising the fidelity of uncertainty estimates.

papers.title: Can LLM Agents Be Forward-Deployed Engineers? Requirement Discovery and Delivery for Enterprise Text-to-SQL
papers.abstract: LLM coding agents can increasingly automate model post-training, but whether they can act as forward-deployed engineer (FDE) agents, discovering customer requirements and turning them into deployment decisions, remains unclear. We study this on a real enterprise text-to-SQL engagement: a simulated customer, grounded in the real use case's requirements, starts with an ambiguous request. An agent must discover acceptance criteria, data permissions, and hardware constraints in the discovery phase, then plan and execute a post-training recipe in the delivery phase. Across 15 models, the strongest discover over 80% of withheld requirements and open-weight models discover 40-50%; in the delivery phase, only 25% of runs across eight coding-agent configurations pass all acceptance criteria. We identify four bottlenecks in this engagement: (1) incomplete discovery, with 40% of withheld requirements missing or misrepresented; (2) unreliable execution; (3) underused compute budgets and a lack of systematic comparisons across base models and post-training methods; and (4) benchmark accuracy does not guarantee production readiness. We suggest human review of discovered requirements, monitoring of the agent's plan during execution, and an explicit experiment-environment specification covering hardware, budget scope, and production checks.
papers.what_changed: The authors introduce a framework to evaluate LLM agents as forward-deployed engineers (FDEs) that perform requirement discovery and post-training execution in enterprise text-to-SQL tasks. They demonstrate that while top models can discover over 80% of requirements, only 25% of agent executions successfully meet all production acceptance criteria.
papers.why_it_matters: This research is critical for enterprises considering AI for automated software engineering, as it highlights that high performance on traditional benchmarks does not guarantee production readiness and identifies specific gaps in current agent capabilities.

explanations.plain: Imagine hiring an intern to build a custom computer program for your business. You give them a vague idea, and they are responsible for asking the right questions to understand what you need, checking the technical rules, and then actually building the software. This paper tests whether AI agents can act as this kind of 'forward-deployed engineer.' The researchers found that while AI is getting better at asking the right questions, it struggles to finish the job reliably. Think of it like a student who creates a great project outline but makes too many errors when actually typing the code. The authors conclude that AI is not quite ready to work unsupervised in a corporate office, as it still requires human oversight to ensure things work correctly.
explanations.student: This study evaluates LLM agents operating in the role of forward-deployed engineers (FDEs) within an enterprise text-to-SQL pipeline. The agent lifecycle is divided into a discovery phase, where it must elicit requirements (data permissions, hardware constraints, and acceptance criteria) from an ambiguous prompt, and a delivery phase, involving model post-training execution. The authors test 15 models, finding a notable disparity: top models reach 80% requirement discovery, but only 25% of deployment runs satisfy all constraints. The researchers pinpoint four primary bottlenecks: incomplete discovery (40% of requirements often missed), unreliable execution, inefficient compute resource allocation, and a decoupling between standard benchmark accuracy and production readiness. The study emphasizes that current benchmarks fail to capture the multi-turn, multi-constraint nature of real-world software engineering. They advocate for a shift toward structured 'experiment-environment specifications' and human-in-the-loop validation for requirement gathering to bridge the gap between agent prototyping and production deployment.
explanations.expert: The paper presents a systematic evaluation of LLM agents as FDEs tasked with full-cycle enterprise text-to-SQL development, encompassing requirement elicitation and automated post-training. Evaluation of 15 models reveals a significant performance delta: while frontier models achieve >80% recall on withheld requirement criteria, open-weight models hover between 40-50%. The delivery phase shows a low success rate, with only 25% of runs across eight agent configurations meeting the stipulated acceptance criteria. The authors identify four bottlenecks: (1) high rates of hallucinated or missing requirements (40% failure rate in discovery); (2) stochasticity in execution; (3) suboptimal compute budget utilization; and (4) the 'benchmark gap,' where high scores on static datasets like Spider do not correlate with production-level system reliability. The methodology suggests that current agentic workflows lack necessary structural constraints. The authors recommend adopting explicit environment specifications that define hardware, cost, and functional validation bounds. This work highlights that model performance is currently insufficient for autonomous software delivery without integrated human oversight and rigorous monitoring of agent planning trajectories.

papers.title: PianoBench: Evaluating Musical Perception and Reasoning in Language Models
papers.abstract: Multimodal language models continue to improve on broad music understanding benchmarks, but which musical features can they perceive and reason about? We investigate this question by introducing PianoBench, a benchmark that tasks language models with reasoning about musical performances across congruent acoustic and symbolic input representations. PianoBench is derived from our new multimodal, training-scale dataset comprising more than 20,000 hours of interleaved transcripts of music and spoken musical commentary from instructional piano videos. Open-weight audio-language models achieve at most 52.8% accuracy on PianoBench, and at best only modestly outperform their accuracy on a no-audio control. In contrast, frontier models using chain of thought achieve up to 93.2% accuracy when provided transcripts of music as text, exposing a gap between perceiving musical features from audio and reasoning about musical events when they are given explicitly. We then test whether mid-training on interleaved musical instruction can improve question answering without chain of thought, raising Qwen 3.5 9B Base's zero-shot accuracy on PianoBench with music transcripts from 42.8% to 56.0% after instruction tuning. These experiments suggest that instructional videos may represent an overlooked source of multimodal supervision for music. Available: https://gclef-cmu.org/pianobench.
papers.what_changed: The authors introduce PianoBench, a benchmark for evaluating musical perception and reasoning using 20,000 hours of interleaved audio-transcript data. They demonstrate that open-weight models struggle with audio perception (max 52.8% accuracy) compared to text-based reasoning (up to 93.2% accuracy) and show that instruction tuning on music datasets improves model performance.
papers.why_it_matters: Researchers and developers in multimodal AI can use this to identify why current models struggle with audio-based musical reasoning compared to text-based inputs, helping refine future model training.

explanations.plain: AI models are getting better at understanding music, but we do not know if they truly 'hear' music or just recognize patterns. The researchers created PianoBench, a new test based on 20,000 hours of piano instructional videos, to see if models can reason about musical events. They found that while models perform very well when given written descriptions of music, they fail to reach the same level when they have to listen to the actual audio. Think of it like a student who can pass a written test on music theory perfectly but cannot recognize the notes when hearing a live piano performance. This shows that while models are good at processing text, they still struggle to connect sounds to musical concepts in the same way.
explanations.student: PianoBench is a new benchmark designed to evaluate how multimodal language models perceive and reason about music using dual input modes: acoustic audio and symbolic (text) transcripts. The dataset consists of over 20,000 hours of instructional piano video transcripts. The authors identify a significant performance gap: while frontier models achieve up to 93.2% accuracy using text-based transcripts, open-weight models max out at 52.8% on audio tasks. This suggests a failure in audio-to-musical-reasoning capability rather than a fundamental lack of musical logic. To mitigate this, the researchers experimented with mid-training (instruction tuning) on interleaved musical content. They specifically applied this to the Qwen 3.5 9B Base model, which saw its zero-shot accuracy increase from 42.8% to 56.0% on text-based transcripts. This highlights that while models can perform complex reasoning tasks when given explicit text, they currently lack robust cross-modal grounding for audio, which can be partially addressed through targeted multimodal instruction tuning.
explanations.expert: PianoBench provides a structured evaluation framework for musical reasoning using a corpus of 20,000 hours of audio-transcript pairs derived from instructional piano videos. The evaluation compares performance across audio-conditioned inputs and text-transcripts, revealing a significant disparity in model capabilities. Experimental results show that current open-weight multimodal models achieve a maximum accuracy of 52.8% on audio inputs, with negligible gains over no-audio control tasks, suggesting poor integration of acoustic features. Conversely, frontier models leveraging chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning achieve 93.2% accuracy on symbolic (text) inputs. The authors investigate if instruction tuning on interleaved musical datasets can enhance reasoning capabilities in the absence of CoT. Testing on Qwen 3.5 9B Base, they report an improvement in zero-shot accuracy from 42.8% to 56.0% post-instruction tuning on music transcripts. The results underscore that although scaling laws and CoT provide strong reasoning benchmarks, there is a clear deficit in extracting and representing high-level musical semantics directly from audio signals. This work advocates for the use of large-scale instructional video corpora as a source of multimodal supervision to bridge the perception-reasoning gap.

papers.title: MonoLaDN: Language-Guided DeNoising for Monocular 3D Object Detection
papers.abstract: Monocular 3D object detection offers a low-cost route to 3D perception, but it remains fundamentally ill-posed, since depth must be inferred from a single view. Recent transformer-based detectors learn geometry purely from image features and 3D box annotations, lacking the high-level semantic priors that vision-language models (VLMs) acquire from large-scale pretraining. VLMs offer such priors, but deploying one directly as a detector is impractical due to its heavy inference cost. We propose MonoLaDN, a language-guided denoising framework that transfers the geometric reasoning of a VLM into a monocular 3D detector while keeping the deployed model purely vision-based. During training, a frozen VLM produces structured reasoning about each object's occlusion, depth, dimension, and angle from the image and its ground-truth boxes. We encode this reasoning into queries, perturb them with noise, and train the detector to reconstruct the clean reasoning. Reconstructing the corrupted reasoning forces the detector's depth-guided features to internalize the VLM's geometric priors, so this knowledge remains available even after the reasoning path is discarded at inference, adding no latency or parameters to the deployed model. Experiments on KITTI 3D and nuScenes show that MonoLaDN consistently outperforms state-of-the-art detectors and generalizes well to new domains.
papers.what_changed: MonoLaDN introduces a language-guided denoising framework that distills geometric reasoning from a frozen VLM into a monocular 3D detector. The method uses VLM-generated object descriptions to train the detector to reconstruct reasoning, allowing the final model to retain geometric priors without the inference cost of a VLM.
papers.why_it_matters: This approach enables efficient 3D perception by injecting rich semantic and geometric knowledge from heavy models into lightweight detectors, providing better accuracy for self-driving applications without slowing down inference.

explanations.plain: Self-driving cars often use cameras to judge how far objects are from them. This is hard because cameras lose depth information when flattening a 3D world into a 2D picture. While large AI models that read text and look at images are good at guessing depth, they are too slow and bulky to run inside a moving vehicle. MonoLaDN solves this by using a large, smart model as a tutor. During training, the tutor explains the distance and size of objects to a smaller, faster model. Once the smaller model learns these lessons, it doesn't need the tutor anymore. It is like a student who learns to solve math problems by copying a teacher's logic and can then pass the final test alone.
explanations.student: Monocular 3D object detection is inherently ill-posed because it requires recovering 3D spatial information from a 2D image. Recent transformer-based architectures often struggle to learn robust geometry from limited annotations. MonoLaDN addresses this by using a form of knowledge distillation from a pretrained Vision-Language Model (VLM). The core idea is to treat geometric properties like depth, occlusion, and object dimensions as semantic concepts the VLM can reason about. During the training phase, the authors freeze the VLM and use its output to create structured reasoning tokens. These tokens are perturbed with noise, creating a denoising task for the primary 3D detector. By learning to reconstruct the clean, VLM-informed reasoning, the detector updates its internal feature representations to align with the VLM's spatial understanding. Critically, this process is strictly for training. Because the VLM and the reasoning reconstruction path are discarded at inference, the method adds zero latency or parameter overhead to the deployed detector. This effectively injects high-level geometric priors into a purely vision-based pipeline, resulting in significant performance gains on standard benchmarks like KITTI and nuScenes.
explanations.expert: MonoLaDN addresses the geometric ambiguity in monocular 3D object detection by distilling structural geometric priors from a frozen VLM into a standard transformer-based detector. The framework treats VLM-generated structured reasoning (occlusion, depth, dimension, and angular orientation) as ground-truth proxies. These reasoning outputs are encoded into queries and subjected to noise; the detector is then optimized to reconstruct the noise-free reasoning. This encourages the detector's latent features to map directly to the geometric nuances identified by the VLM. The architecture maintains a pure vision-based pipeline during inference, eliminating the computational bottleneck associated with running large VLMs in real-time. Experimental results on the KITTI 3D and nuScenes datasets demonstrate that the proposed denoising task leads to consistent improvements over current state-of-the-art detectors. By forcing the model to internalize geometric priors through reconstruction, the method exhibits strong cross-domain generalization. The primary limitation of this approach is its reliance on the VLM's initial capability to reason about 3D properties from image inputs, as the detector's performance is upper-bounded by the quality and accuracy of the VLM-generated guidance.

papers.title: Polynomial-Time Computation of Extensive-Form Proper Equilibria in Two-Player Zero-Sum Games
papers.abstract: We give a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm for computing an exact extensive-form proper equilibrium in a finite two-player zero-sum extensive-form game with perfect recall and rational data. Properness is understood in the agent normal form: an action at an information set is penalized relative to a better action while all other local behavioral choices, including the player's own future actions, remain fixed. Our algorithm assigns each information set a geometric permutahedron of allowable action probabilities. A scaled doubly stochastic representation embeds these restrictions in a polynomial-size sequence-form polytope; a saddle point then satisfies the local $\varepsilon$-properness inequalities. To obtain an exact equilibrium rather than a solution at an arbitrarily small numerical perturbation, we establish sign stability of a parametric linear system, construct a persistent feasible basis, and extract the limits of behavioral ratios. The resulting probabilities are rational and have polynomial encoding length, including at information sets whose realization probabilities vanish.
papers.what_changed: The paper introduces a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm to compute exact extensive-form proper equilibria in two-player zero-sum games with perfect recall. It achieves this by using a scaled doubly stochastic representation of action probabilities within a sequence-form polytope and solving a parametric linear system to ensure exactness.
papers.why_it_matters: This result solves a long-standing complexity challenge in game theory, offering a way to compute refined equilibria, which are more robust than standard Nash equilibria, efficiently for games where realization probabilities may approach zero.

explanations.plain: In game theory, a Nash equilibrium describes a state where no player can benefit by changing their strategy alone. However, some equilibria are unstable or rely on 'weak' moves that wouldn't actually be made. A 'proper' equilibrium is a stricter version that filters out these nonsensical moves by assuming players make mistakes only with extremely low probability. Previously, calculating these refined solutions was difficult or required messy approximations. This research introduces a new mathematical method that guarantees finding the perfect solution in a predictable, efficient amount of time. Think of it like finding the most reliable path through a complex maze: instead of guessing and checking every possible turn, this method uses a structured geometric map to pinpoint the exact, optimal route without needing to approximate.
explanations.student: The paper addresses the computation of proper equilibria in extensive-form games (EFGs) with perfect recall. While Nash equilibria are foundational, they often include strategies that are not robust to small perturbations. A proper equilibrium, defined here in the agent normal form, introduces a refinement that penalizes sub-optimal actions at information sets. The author utilizes the sequence-form representation, a common technique to handle the exponential number of pure strategies in EFGs by representing policies through realization probabilities. The core technical contribution is a polynomial-time algorithm that maps information sets to a geometric permutahedron of action probabilities. By embedding these into a sequence-form polytope and utilizing a scaled doubly stochastic representation, the author ensures that the local epsilon-properness inequalities are satisfied. Crucially, the paper moves beyond numerical approximation by solving a parametric linear system. By establishing the sign stability of this system and constructing a persistent feasible basis, the algorithm extracts exact rational probabilities. This demonstrates that an exact solution exists with a polynomial encoding length, even when realization probabilities vanish, a common issue in extensive-form equilibrium computation.
explanations.expert: This paper presents a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm for computing an exact proper equilibrium in two-player zero-sum extensive-form games (EFGs) with perfect recall and rational data. Properness is defined via the agent normal form, where local behavioral choices at information sets are subject to specific penalties relative to better actions. The methodology maps each information set to a geometric permutahedron of allowable probabilities, subsequently integrated into a sequence-form polytope via a scaled doubly stochastic representation. The algorithm addresses the convergence issue inherent in epsilon-properness by treating the problem as a parametric linear system. By proving the sign stability of this system, the author constructs a persistent feasible basis that allows for the extraction of exact limits for behavioral ratios as the perturbation parameter approaches zero. A significant result is the demonstration that these probabilities are rational and possess polynomial encoding length, even at information sets where the realization probability is zero. This effectively bridges the gap between approximate epsilon-equilibrium computation and exact refinement. The work is particularly relevant for practitioners dealing with strategy robustness and equilibrium refinement in large-scale strategic interactions where standard Nash solutions may be non-discriminatory regarding player mistakes.

papers.title: Neural Compression over Equivalence Classes: Exact Gauges and Functional Rate-Distortion
papers.abstract: Neural networks admit many parameterizations of the same or nearly the same function, but deployment typically stores whichever parameter vector training happens to produce. We show that this representational freedom can itself be used for compression. Rather than redesigning the codec, we search over exact function-preserving transformations and controlled functional perturbations, using the unchanged physical compressor itself to select cheaper representations. Exact gauge families provide a zero-distortion reference under the strict audit; allowing small functional changes exposes much larger rate-distortion gains. Across SmolLM2 and Qwen3, our method reduces Zstandard-compressed checkpoint size by up to 23.4\%, with similar relative reductions under gzip, Brotli, and ZipNN, establishing trained-network representational freedom as a practical storage resource.
papers.what_changed: The paper introduces a method to compress neural network checkpoints by searching for parameterizations within equivalence classes that minimize storage size. By utilizing exact gauge transformations and functional perturbations, it achieves up to 23.4% reduction in Zstandard-compressed checkpoint sizes for models like SmolLM2 and Qwen3.
papers.why_it_matters: Practitioners managing large language model checkpoints can significantly reduce storage and bandwidth costs without needing to redesign existing compression codecs like gzip or Zstandard.

explanations.plain: Modern artificial intelligence models are often huge files, making them difficult to store and share. This paper uses a clever trick: many different sets of internal numbers can result in the exact same AI behavior. Imagine you have a complex mathematical problem to solve. You could write the answer in many different ways, like using fractions, decimals, or different algebraic arrangements. Some versions take up more ink on the page than others. The researchers found that by carefully rewriting the internal 'math' of an AI model to use the most compact representation possible, they can shrink the file size significantly. It is like finding a way to rewrite a long book using a specialized shorthand that fits the same story into a much smaller notebook.
explanations.student: Neural networks are over-parameterized, meaning different weight configurations can represent identical or near-identical functions. This is known as representational freedom. This research exploits this property to improve model compression without changing the underlying architecture or requiring a custom codec. The authors leverage exact gauge families, transformations that preserve the network function, to find representations that are more compressible by standard algorithms like Zstandard, gzip, or Brotli. By defining a functional rate-distortion trade-off, they allow for controlled, minimal functional perturbations to optimize the representation for bit-rate reduction. Essentially, they treat the model parameters as a signal and search for a transformation within the equivalence class that maximizes compression efficiency under existing lossless algorithms. The results show that this approach achieves up to a 23.4% reduction in file size for modern models like SmolLM2 and Qwen3. This demonstrates that we can treat the inherent redundancy in neural network weight spaces as a valuable resource for data compression rather than just an artifact of training.
explanations.expert: The paper addresses representational redundancy in deep neural networks by optimizing parameter vectors within their equivalence classes to maximize compressibility. The author utilizes exact gauge symmetries and controlled functional perturbations to minimize the rate-distortion objective under off-the-shelf compressors such as Zstandard, gzip, Brotli, and ZipNN. Unlike traditional post-training quantization, this method focuses on finding a transformation $f$ such that the encoded size of the parameter vector $\theta'$ is minimized, where $\theta'$ belongs to an equivalence class yielding an identical or functionally proximal mapping. By searching for a gauge that minimizes the entropy of the resulting representation, the method achieves up to a 23.4% reduction in checkpoint file size for SmolLM2 and Qwen3 models. This is achieved without architectural modification, relying instead on the representational freedom inherent in current over-parameterized regimes. The study provides an empirical validation of using functional equivalence as a practical resource for model storage, with a clear trade-off between exact function preservation (zero-distortion) and controlled functional approximation (higher compression). Limitations include the computational cost of the search process, though the method is non-invasive to existing inference pipelines.

papers.title: Interactive World Simulation with Cosmos for Physical AI
papers.abstract: We present a shared framework that adapts Cosmos world foundation models for real-time interactive world simulation in Physical AI. By streaming visual observations in response to actions and scene controls, the framework enables users and embodied agents to interact with evolving virtual environments. It supports both predicting the visual consequences of actions and generating observations from physical state maintained by an external simulator. We demonstrate this approach across camera navigation and robot manipulation, controllable video transfer, and multi-view autonomous vehicle (AV) simulation. These examples provide a shared foundation for developing interactive virtual environments for Physical AI training and evaluation. Our code and model checkpoints are available at https://github.com/nvidia/cosmos and https://huggingface.co/collections/nvidia/cosmos3-examples. The project website is available at https://research.nvidia.com/labs/cosmos-lab/cosmos-simulation.
papers.what_changed: The authors introduce a framework that adapts Cosmos world foundation models to provide real-time, interactive simulation by processing action-based visual feedback and external physical state inputs.
papers.why_it_matters: Researchers and robotics engineers can use this platform to create interactive training environments for embodied AI, bridging the gap between static generative models and active physical simulation.

explanations.plain: Imagine you are playing a video game where the world reacts to your moves instantly, but instead of the game being programmed by hand, an AI creates the scenery on the fly. This paper introduces a system that turns 'world models', which usually just predict what comes next in a video, into interactive playgrounds. By allowing the AI to 'see' actions and control commands, it can simulate how a robot arm moves or how a car navigates a street in real time. Think of it like a smart simulator that acts like a movie director, constantly filming and adjusting the scene based on how you interact with the environment, which is vital for teaching robots how to behave in the real world.
explanations.student: The paper presents a framework to transition Cosmos-based world foundation models from passive predictive tasks to active, interactive simulation. A world model is a generative architecture trained to predict future visual states based on past observations. By incorporating action inputs and scene controls, this framework allows for a closed-loop system where visual observations are streamed in response to agent behavior. The architecture supports two modes: predicting the visual consequences of an agent's actions directly, or generating observations conditioned on physical states tracked by an external physics simulator. This approach is demonstrated across several domains, including robotics manipulation, camera navigation, and multi-view autonomous vehicle simulation. By providing a shared foundation for both generation and simulation, the work facilitates the creation of virtual environments for training embodied AI. The implementation allows practitioners to leverage these foundation models to evaluate agents in environments where the visual output remains consistent with the underlying physical dynamics of the scene.
explanations.expert: This work introduces an interactive simulation framework built upon Cosmos world foundation models, enabling real-time visual grounding for physical AI. The system architectures support two primary operational paradigms: action-conditioned visual sequence generation and state-conditioned rendering derived from external physics engines. This enables the model to function as a bridge between high-fidelity generative visual output and low-level physical dynamics. The authors demonstrate the utility of this approach across distinct domains: robot manipulation, controllable video generation, and autonomous vehicle multi-view simulation. By integrating action priors and scene-level control tokens into the Cosmos architecture, the model maintains temporal and spatial consistency during interactive sequences. This framework provides a scalable alternative to traditional simulation environments, allowing for the generation of diverse, interactive training data for embodied agents. The approach is validated through the release of model checkpoints and source code, providing a baseline for evaluating foundation models in active, rather than merely observational, settings. Limitations include reliance on the base model's capacity to represent long-range physical consistency and the fidelity of the external simulator integration.

papers.title: Goal Revelation as a Bridge Between Information-Theoretic Empowerment and Capability-Based Human Power
papers.abstract: Power matters for AI safety. Optimal agents tend to acquire power across a wide range of objectives (instrumental convergence). As we embed AI agents into socio-technical systems, humans risk gradual disempowerment. Both concerns call for a formal, quantitative measure of power. Two such measures in the context of Markov games are information-theoretic empowerment, the capacity of the channel from an agent's actions to future states, and capability-based individual power, a measure of goal attainment built from the probabilities that a human would attain each goal in a family of candidates were they pursuing it. We show where the two meet. From individual power, Fano's inequality yields a floor $B(s)$. This floor is a lower bound on what we term goal revelation, the mutual information $\mathbb{I}(G;ξ\mid s)$ between the human's latent goal and the realised trajectory. Empowerment caps revelation from above, so that $B(s) \le \mathbb{I}(G;ξ\mid s) \le \mathbb{I}(\mathbf{A}_h \to ξ\mid s) \le \mathfrak{E}_h(s)$. Each quantity can be large while the one below it stays at zero, highlighting the following failure modes. An assistant maximising empowerment can prefer an interface offering broad influence over goal-irrelevant degrees of freedom to one that lets the human attain every goal they might hold. An assistant maximising revelation cannot tell a working interface from one rewired so that every goal yields the wrong outcome, since relabelling goals leaves mutual information unchanged while zeroing every attainment probability. Positive guarantees therefore come only from the attainment end of the chain. A satisfaction floor, computable from two statistics of interaction logs, offers a way to monitor the power users retain in a deployed system, and simulations in random environments show the three quantities are correlated but far from interchangeable.
papers.what_changed: The paper introduces the concept of goal revelation and defines a mathematical chain of inequalities relating information-theoretic empowerment, goal revelation, and capability-based power. It demonstrates that these metrics are not interchangeable and proposes a satisfaction floor based on interaction logs to monitor user power.
papers.why_it_matters: Researchers and developers building AI assistants need this framework to understand how AI power impacts human autonomy. It provides a formal way to ensure AI systems do not inadvertently reduce human agency, highlighting why simple metrics like information flow are insufficient.

explanations.plain: As AI becomes more integrated into our lives, a major concern is whether we are losing control over our decisions. This paper explores how to measure 'power' in human-AI systems. Imagine you have a remote control for your house. Power could be measured by how many buttons it has, or by how well those buttons actually work to do what you want. The authors show that just having a lot of influence over a system (like having many buttons) does not mean you can effectively reach your goals. They propose a way to monitor this balance, ensuring that as AI grows more capable, it remains a tool that truly serves human objectives rather than just expanding its own range of influence.
explanations.student: The paper analyzes the relationship between two formal metrics of power in Markov games: information-theoretic empowerment (the capacity of the action-state channel) and capability-based individual power (attainability of goal sets). The authors introduce 'goal revelation,' defined as the mutual information between a latent goal and the realized trajectory. By applying Fano’s inequality, they derive a chain of inequalities linking these metrics: a satisfaction floor, goal revelation, and empowerment. The key insight is that these quantities are distinct. For instance, maximizing empowerment may lead to broad influence over irrelevant variables, while maximizing revelation is insensitive to 'goal relabeling', a scenario where a system successfully communicates information but fails to reach the correct goal states. Consequently, they argue that positive safety guarantees require focusing on attainment rather than pure information flow. They propose a 'satisfaction floor' metric, which is computable from interaction logs, to track human empowerment in real-world systems. Simulations show that while these metrics correlate, they capture fundamentally different aspects of power dynamics, demonstrating that system designers must distinguish between control and effective goal realization.
explanations.expert: This research provides a formal framework for assessing power dynamics in socio-technical systems, specifically within Markov games. The authors establish a hierarchy of power measures: the satisfaction floor B(s), goal revelation I(G;ξ|s), and information-theoretic empowerment E_h(s). Using Fano's inequality, they derive the chain B(s) ≤ I(G;ξ|s) ≤ I(A_h → ξ|s) ≤ E_h(s). The work identifies critical failure modes: empowerment-maximizing agents may prioritize entropy over utility, while revelation-maximizing agents ignore goal-attainment failure due to the invariance of mutual information under goal relabeling. The paper formally demonstrates why these quantities are not interchangeable, confirming that empowerment is a necessary but insufficient condition for goal attainment. The authors propose a satisfaction floor derived from two statistics of interaction logs, providing a scalable diagnostic tool for deployment. Limitations include the reliance on specific Markov game definitions and the analytical focus on theoretical bounds. Simulations across random environments illustrate the divergence of these metrics, suggesting that AI safety practitioners should monitor capability-based attainment directly rather than relying on information-theoretic proxies to prevent unintended human disempowerment.

papers.title: SeVerus: Context-Aware, Gamified Benchmarking for Rust Verification
papers.abstract: Coding agents achieve high success rates on existing benchmarks for Verus, a verifier for Rust programs. These benchmarks typically provide the auxiliary lemmas needed to complete a proof. In practice, however, such lemmas must be discovered and proved. To capture this challenge, we present SEVERUS, a context-aware technique to generate Verus benchmarks that organizes verification tasks into quests, each divided into levelsin a gamified manner. Using the original proof dependencies in verified projects, SEVERUS constructs one quest per verification target and progressively removes proof context to create individual levels. These levels range from the easiest, requiring completing only a single missing lemma, to the hardest, requiring proving the target without any supporting lemmas. An independent checker rejects changes to executable code, weakened specifications, and unsound proof constructs. A noisy binary search estimates the highest level that an agent can solve reliably. Applied to six open-source Verus projects, SEVERUS generates 819 quests comprising 10,095 levels. Experiments with Codex using GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna, and with Claude Code using Sonnet 4.6, show that success decreases and cost increases as proof context is withdrawn. The strongest agent solves the final level of 52 of 60 sampled quests, yet can only reliably solve 35% of their levels, with failures concentrated in longer quests. Successful GPT-6 Sol proofs rarely reproduce the withheld lemmas, instead, using alternative proof decompositions. By systematically varying proof context, SEVERUS provides a foundation for constructing verification benchmarks that can continue to challenge increasingly capable coding agents.
papers.what_changed: The authors introduce SEVERUS, a framework that generates context-aware, gamified verification benchmarks by systematically removing proof dependencies from existing verified Rust projects to create levels of increasing difficulty.
papers.why_it_matters: It forces AI coding agents to prove programs from scratch rather than relying on provided auxiliary lemmas, providing a more realistic and rigorous test for verification capabilities.

explanations.plain: Writing software that is guaranteed to be error-free is difficult. Often, programmers use special tools to mathematically prove their code works. Usually, AI helpers perform well at this because they are given 'hints' or building blocks called lemmas to finish the proof. SEVERUS acts like a video game developer that takes these full proofs and breaks them into quests with increasing difficulty. In the early levels, the AI gets some hints, but in the final levels, it must prove the code from scratch. Think of it like a math student who is usually allowed to look at the answer key. SEVERUS slowly takes the answer key away, forcing the AI to actually understand the logic rather than just filling in the blanks.
explanations.student: Formal verification using tools like Verus often involves proving complex Rust properties. Current benchmarks for coding agents typically provide the necessary auxiliary lemmas, which simplifies the task significantly. SEVERUS addresses this by creating a gamified benchmark suite that deconstructs existing proof dependencies. It organizes verification targets into quests consisting of multiple levels. Level generation is achieved by progressively stripping away auxiliary lemmas from the original project proofs. This results in a spectrum of difficulty, ranging from completing a single lemma to full verification. The system uses a noisy binary search to estimate the agent's reliability threshold across these levels. An independent checker ensures validity by rejecting code changes, weakened specifications, or unsound proof constructs. By testing agents like Codex and Claude, the study demonstrates that success rates drop significantly as proof context is reduced, highlighting a gap in current agent performance when solving complex verification tasks without guidance. The findings show that agents often find alternative proof paths rather than reproducing the original lemmas, providing a robust, scalable way to evaluate the reasoning capabilities of future coding models.
explanations.expert: SEVERUS provides a methodology for systematic benchmarking of LLM-based coding agents in the context of the Verus verifier. It addresses the limitation of current benchmarks, where auxiliary lemmas are provided as context, by automating the decomposition of verified Rust projects into 819 quests and 10,095 levels. SEVERUS constructs these levels by pruning proof dependencies, effectively modulating the context availability. It utilizes an independent checker to ensure the integrity of the executable code and specifications. Evaluation of models including GPT-6 Sol, GPT-6 Luna, and Claude Sonnet 4.6 reveals that agent reliability significantly declines as the level of required independent proof increases. Specifically, the strongest agent successfully solves the final level of 52 of 60 sampled quests, yet only maintains a 35% reliability rate across all levels. A key observation is that agents rarely reconstruct the original withheld lemmas, opting instead for alternative proof decompositions. This work establishes a quantitative framework for measuring the 'proof capability' of LLMs under varying levels of structural assistance, revealing that performance degradation is particularly acute in longer, more complex proof quests.

papers.title: Symmetry Breaking at the Edge of Stability via Central Flow Analysis
papers.abstract: Continuous symmetries in neural networks lead to conserved quantities that are invariant under gradient flow, such as layer balancedness in linear and ReLU networks. Finite-step gradient descent need not preserve these laws, particularly at the edge of stability (EOS), where the iterates oscillate around a smoother trajectory, which can be described by the central flow dynamics (Cohen et al., 2025). We study how gradient flow conservation laws evolve under the central flow description of this regime. We show that the curvature correction induces a finite-dimensional drift determined by the oscillation covariance along critical parameter directions. We thus take the first steps to analyse which conservation laws remain and are broken at the EOS according to the central flow dynamics by analysing a scalar two-layer model, two-layer matrix factorisation, and a two-layer ReLU network, where the known conservation laws are shown to be complete (Marcotte et al., 2023).
papers.what_changed: The authors introduce a central flow analysis to demonstrate that curvature corrections at the edge of stability cause a finite-dimensional drift that breaks established gradient flow conservation laws.
papers.why_it_matters: Researchers and deep learning theorists should care because this explains why neural networks behave differently during training when learning rates are large, potentially impacting our understanding of model stability.

explanations.plain: Imagine you are trying to keep a heavy ball perfectly balanced on the top of a mountain. In an ideal world, the laws of physics might guarantee the ball stays put. However, if the ground begins to vibrate or tilt rapidly, what scientists call the edge of stability, those guarantees no longer hold. This paper looks at how neural networks 'learn' during training. Usually, there are strict mathematical rules that dictate how the network's internal connections should change over time. The authors found that when the training is pushed to this unstable edge, the network starts vibrating in a way that breaks these rules. It is like a train that was supposed to stay on its tracks but begins to drift because the ground itself is shifting.
explanations.student: In deep learning, neural networks often exhibit symmetries that result in conserved quantities during gradient flow, such as balanced layer weights. This behaviour is typically modeled by continuous differential equations. However, standard discrete gradient descent steps, especially at the 'edge of stability' (EOS) where the learning rate causes iterates to oscillate, do not strictly preserve these invariants. The authors employ 'central flow', a mathematical framework that approximates the jagged, oscillatory path of EOS training with a smoother, secondary trajectory. By analyzing a scalar model, matrix factorization, and a two-layer ReLU network, they demonstrate that curvature corrections at the EOS introduce a specific drift. This drift is quantified by the oscillation covariance along critical directions, proving that these previously stable conservation laws are fundamentally broken in the high-learning-rate regime. The study confirms that while these laws are complete in the standard continuous limit, the discretization and oscillation effects inherent in the EOS introduce new, measurable dynamics.
explanations.expert: The paper investigates the breaking of gradient flow conservation laws in neural networks when training at the edge of stability (EOS). Utilizing the central flow framework (Cohen et al., 2025), the authors define a continuous-time approximation for the oscillatory training regime. They derive that the second-order curvature correction induces a deterministic drift proportional to the oscillation covariance along critical parameter directions. The analysis evaluates three specific architectures: a scalar two-layer model, a two-layer matrix factorization model, and a two-layer ReLU network. Building on the completeness of conservation laws defined in Marcotte et al. (2023), the paper demonstrates that the EOS regime is not merely a discretization artifact but involves the systematic violation of these invariants. The results provide a theoretical foundation for understanding how the loss landscape's local curvature and the optimization hyperparameters drive the divergence from continuous-time expectations. Limitations include the focus on restricted, low-capacity architectures, though the framework identifies the mechanism by which higher-order dynamics influence optimization paths.

papers.title: Does Frontier AI Strengthen Cyber Defense? Evidence from Project Glasswing
papers.abstract: Defenders and attackers race to find the same software flaws. I use the launch of Project Glasswing, which gave a small group of large US tech firms early access to Claude Mythos Preview, a model for finding software vulnerabilities, to study how access to frontier AI affects defenders, external researchers, and attackers. Using the universe of publicly disclosed vulnerabilities, I find that firms with access more than doubled their disclosures relative to Chinese and Russian tech firms without access, disclosed about 150 percent more high-impact vulnerabilities, and fixed reported flaws as quickly as before. As treated firms found more flaws themselves, external researchers, who sell their findings through bug bounties, reported about half as many vulnerabilities in treated firms' code and more in other firms' code, without leaving the market. There is no evidence that attackers exploited the additional vulnerabilities: the share exploited within a month of disclosure fell by about two thirds, mainly because a smaller share was already exploited when disclosed, while the number exploited did not change. Frontier AI helped defenders find and fix more flaws before attackers exploited them, but its restricted release creates an asymmetry in software security between firms in different countries.
papers.what_changed: This paper analyzes the launch of Project Glasswing, finding that access to the Claude Mythos Preview AI model caused participating firms to more than double their vulnerability disclosures and identify 150 percent more high-impact flaws compared to firms without access.
papers.why_it_matters: Policy makers and cybersecurity professionals should care because this provides evidence that frontier AI can significantly enhance defensive capabilities without creating a net increase in successful cyber attacks, while highlighting potential geopolitical security asymmetries.

explanations.plain: Imagine software like a giant, complex house with thousands of hidden windows. Cybersecurity researchers act like inspectors trying to find unlocked windows so they can be locked before burglars find them. In this study, a group of tech companies was given a powerful AI tool to help them hunt for these unlocked windows. The results show that these companies found and fixed many more vulnerabilities than companies without the tool. Surprisingly, the burglars did not seem to get an edge from this; instead, the companies got a head start on closing security gaps. It is like giving a homeowner a high-tech flashlight to find weak spots in their security before anyone else notices, making their home safer without helping the thieves.
explanations.student: This study investigates the impact of large language model (LLM) assisted vulnerability research on software security ecosystems. The research tracks Project Glasswing, an initiative providing firms with early access to Claude Mythos Preview, a model designed for automated vulnerability discovery. The study employs a comparative analysis between participating firms and non-participating international entities. Key findings include a 150 percent increase in high-impact vulnerability disclosures among treated firms. An interesting dynamic shift is observed in the bug bounty market: external researchers reported fewer vulnerabilities for treated firms, suggesting that the AI-driven internal discovery process effectively catches bugs before external contractors can find them. Crucially, the study evaluates the 'attacker advantage' hypothesis by measuring the exploitation rate within one month post-disclosure. The data indicates that the share of exploited vulnerabilities dropped by approximately two-thirds, suggesting that AI-assisted internal discovery improves the speed and scale of remediation without increasing exploitation risks. The paper concludes that while frontier AI benefits defense, its restricted availability creates a structural security disparity between firms with access and those without.
explanations.expert: This research provides empirical evidence on the impact of frontier AI on the software vulnerability lifecycle. The study analyzes the deployment of Claude Mythos Preview under Project Glasswing, using vulnerability disclosure data to evaluate defensive gains. Treated firms demonstrated a significant increase in security posture, with vulnerability disclosures more than doubling and high-impact flaw identification increasing by 150 percent. The study provides critical evidence regarding the exploitation gap: despite increased internal discovery, the share of vulnerabilities exploited within a one-month window decreased by two-thirds. This indicates that AI-accelerated internal discovery effectively preempts attacker activity. Furthermore, the analysis of bug bounty data shows that external researcher contributions shifted away from treated firms, indicating a substitution effect where internal AI-driven processes capture 'low-hanging fruit' formerly addressed by external bounty hunters. The paper identifies a non-zero-sum outcome for defenders but notes an emerging security asymmetry between firms with access to frontier models and those without. Limitations include the potential for selection bias inherent in the restricted access of Project Glasswing and the reliance on publicly disclosed vulnerability metrics, which may not capture the full spectrum of unobserved private exploitation.

papers.title: Attention Is All You Need
papers.source: 31st Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NIPS 2017)
